title: Fulminant Encephalopathy and Visual Disturbances in Active Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

presentation.chief_complaint: Acute onset headache, visual impairment, dizziness, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures
presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency department with an 8-hour history of severe headache, dizziness, blurry vision, and recurrent generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Each seizure lasted 3 to 4 minutes and was characterized by ocular deviation, jaw clenching, and bilateral upper and lower extremity rigidity followed by brief post-ictal confusion. She was diagnosed with active systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) 3 months prior and developed end-stage renal failure requiring maintenance hemodialysis 2 months ago. Her disease activity has been high (SLEDAI-2K estimated score of 14).
presentation.past_medical_history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (diagnosed 3 months ago based on photosensitivity, arthralgias, cytopenias, ANA 1:640, elevated anti-dsDNA, hypocomplementemia, and lupus anticoagulant positivity); Lupus nephritis causing renal failure on maintenance hemodialysis.
presentation.neuro_exam: Lethargic and oriented only to person. Cranial nerve examination revealed cortical visual impairment with intact pupillary light reflexes; ocular tracking was limited due to altered mental status. Motor exam showed symmetrical withdrawal to painful stimuli with bilateral extensor plantar responses (Babinski signs positive bilaterally). Deep tendon reflexes were hyperactive throughout.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Hemoglobin: 8.2 g/dL, Platelet count: 72,000 /µL, Serum Creatinine: 6.8 mg/dL, BUN: 62 mg/dL, C3 complement: 0.45 g/L (low), C4 complement: 0.06 g/L (low), Anti-dsDNA: >100 IU/mL (elevated), Lupus Anticoagulant: Positive.

A Axial T1-weighted image shows heterogeneous signal intensity in the bilateral parieto-occipital regions with subtle hemorrhagic components. B Axial T2-weighted image demonstrates extensive edema involving the occipital, parietal, and posterior frontal lobes, more pronounced on the right, with evident mass effect. C Axial DWI reveals mixed hyperintensity in the right parieto-occipital area. imaging.findings_summary: Extensive T2 hyperintensity and parieto-occipital mass effect with corresponding DWI hyperintensity and ADC hypointensity, confirming true diffusion restriction and cytotoxic edema alongside microhemorrhagic elements.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Incorrect. Primary CNS vasculitis typically presents subacutely with progressive encephalopathy, multifocal ischemic infarcts of varying ages across multiple arterial territories, and vascular beading on angiographic imaging, rather than rapid onset bilateral parieto-occipital signal changes predominantly localized to posterior regions in the setting of severe hypertension.

Correct! The constellation of severe hypertension, active SLE, renal failure requiring hemodialysis, visual symptoms, seizures, and bilateral parieto-occipital neuroimaging abnormalities is classic for posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). Although PRES typically demonstrates vasogenic edema (high signal on ADC), severe or fulminant cases can exhibit areas of cytotoxic edema (low ADC signal, diffusion restriction) indicating localized tissue ischemia or cytotoxic injury.

options.text: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome-induced acute arterial infarction
options.rationale: Incorrect. While lupus anticoagulant is present, acute arterial ischemic stroke secondary to antiphospholipid syndrome follows a distinct vascular territory (e.g., MCA or PCA thromboembolism). It does not produce widespread, symmetric, confluent subcortical white matter lesions localized across bilateral parieto-occipital regions.

Incorrect. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis typically presents with signs of elevated intracranial pressure, dense sinus signs, or hemorrhagic infarcts non-conforming to arterial boundaries, often adjacent to the superior sagittal or transverse sinuses. MR venography confirms sinus occlusion, which is not described here.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) with Cytotoxic Edema in Severe Active Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is a clinicoradiological entity classically characterized by acute headache, altered mental status, visual disturbance, seizures, and characteristic subcortical parieto-occipital vasogenic edema on neuroimaging. It occurs secondary to defective cerebrovascular autoregulation and endothelial breakdown, commonly triggered by abrupt hypertension, renal dysfunction, cytotoxic therapy, or active systemic autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Although PRES is typically considered a reversible condition with a favorable clinical recovery after blood pressure control and risk factor management, severe autoimmune inflammation and uremia can trigger significant endothelial toxicity and blood-brain barrier disruption.

In severe cases, profound endothelial disruption can cause progression from vasogenic edema to cytotoxic edema, manifested as true diffusion restriction with low values on the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map on MRI. This indicates cellular energy failure and localized irreversible cellular injury. Patients with cytotoxic edema or microhemorrhage in PRES are at elevated risk for permanent neurological deficits, raised intracranial pressure, and complicated clinical courses.
teaching_points: PRES classically manifests as vasogenic edema in parieto-occipital regions, but severe or fulminant cases can show true diffusion restriction (low ADC) representing cytotoxic edema.
Active SLE with renal involvement and uncontrolled hypertension are potent triggers for PRES due to systemic endothelial injury and impaired cerebrovascular autoregulation.
Demonstration of cytotoxic edema or intracranial microhemorrhage in PRES portends a worse clinical prognosis and higher risk of persistent neurological deficits.
clinical_pitfalls: Assuming PRES is always benign and completely reversible, which can lead to underestimating the risk of rapid neurological decline when cytotoxic edema or intracranial bleeding is present.
Misinterpreting diffusion restriction in parieto-occipital regions solely as acute arterial thromboembolic stroke rather than severe PRES with focal cytotoxic ischemia.

title: Painful Left Sixth Nerve Palsy with Orbital Apex Enhancement and Subsequent Constitutional Decline

presentation.chief_complaint: Acute onset of painful left eye pain and horizontal diplopia
presentation.history_of_present_illness: A 70-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of left periorbital pain and horizontal diplopia. He noted a 3-month history of preceding constitutional symptoms, polyarthralgia, unintentional weight loss, and progressive sensorineural hearing loss. During corticosteroid tapering following initial management of his sixth nerve palsy, he developed painful subcutaneous nodules, postprandial abdominal pain, and asymmetric lower extremity weakness with foot drop.
presentation.past_medical_history: Unremarkable prior history aside from constitutional symptoms spanning the preceding 3 months.
presentation.neuro_exam: Left abducens (VI) nerve palsy with associated hyperesthesia in the left ophthalmic (V1) distribution. Subsequent examination revealed tender subcutaneous nodules over the lower limbs and an asymmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex) manifest as a left foot drop and right wrist drop.
presentation.key_labs_csf: ESR 67 mm/h; CRP 42 mg/L. Mild normocytic anemia. ANCA (PR3 and MPO), ANA, complement levels (C3/C4), ACE, lysozyme, and anti-SSA/SSB were negative. Hepatitis B and C serologies negative.

imaging.modality: Axial T1-weighted fat-suppressed post-contrast Brain and Orbital MRI
imaging.caption: Axial T1-weighted, fat-suppressed, post-contrast MRI of the brain and orbits show enhancement in the left orbital apex involving the optic nerve sheath, without well-defined nodularity. The enhancement extends to the superior orbital fissure, the anterior aspect of the cavernous sinus, the pterygopalatine fossa, and the inferior orbital fissure.
imaging.findings_summary: Demonstrates abnormal enhancement in the left orbital apex involving the optic nerve sheath, extending posteriorly through the superior orbital fissure into the anterior cavernous sinus, pterygopalatine fossa, and inferior orbital fissure.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely underlying systemic diagnosis?

options.rationale: Incorrect. Although GPA frequently involves the orbit and cranial nerves, it is classically ANCA-positive (c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA in >80-90% of generalized cases) and characterized by necrotizing granulomatous lesions of the upper and lower respiratory tract.

Incorrect. EGPA typically features prominent adult-onset asthma, severe allergic rhinitis/sinusitis, marked peripheral blood eosinophilia, and p-ANCA positivity in a subset of patients, none of which are described here.

Correct! Polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis that is characteristically ANCA-negative. It features multi-system ischemic involvement, including mononeuritis multiplex (foot/wrist drop), tender cutaneous nodules, postprandial abdominal pain (mesenteric vasculitis), renal vascular involvement, and constitutional decline. Cranial neuropathies and orbital apex syndrome are recognized, albeit uncommon, presenting signs.

Incorrect. While relapsing polychondritis can cause auricular/nasal chondritis, sclera/orbital inflammation, and sensorineural hearing loss, it does not account for tender subcutaneous skin nodules, severe abdominal angina, or classic mononeuritis multiplex.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis affecting medium-sized muscular arteries. It classically spares the pulmonary circulation and is characteristically negative for anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA). Its clinical spectrum includes constitutional decline, tender subcutaneous cutaneous nodules, hypertension, gastrointestinal ischemia (abdominal angina), renal vascular disease, and asymmetric peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex).

Cranial nerve involvement—such as isolated or combined cranial neuropathies associated with orbital apex or cavernous sinus involvement—is a rare presenting sign of systemic vasculitides, including PAN. In this patient, the orbital apex enhancement initially raised suspicion for localized orbital inflammatory disease or Tolosa-Hunt syndrome. However, relapse during steroid tapering with unmasking of systemic multi-organ involvement (mononeuritis multiplex, cutaneous nodules, abdominal angina) pointed definitively to underlying PAN. Tissue biopsy (e.g., skin, nerve, or muscle) or mesenteric angiography confirms the diagnosis. Prompt initiation of high-dose corticosteroids along with cyclophosphamide or steroid-sparing agents is crucial to prevent progressive ischemic neuropathic and end-organ damage.
teaching_points: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis that is characteristically ANCA-negative and spares the pulmonary capillaries.
Cranial neuropathies and orbital apex syndrome can serve as atypical initial presenting manifestations of systemic necrotizing vasculitides.
Development of mononeuritis multiplex, tender cutaneous nodules, and abdominal angina during steroid tapering strongly indicates underlying systemic medium-vessel vasculitis.
clinical_pitfalls: Misdiagnosing cranial neuropathy or orbital apex inflammation as benign idiopathic orbital pseudotumor (Tolosa-Hunt syndrome) without screening for systemic vasculitis.
Failing to recognize systemic relapse symptoms (such as foot drop or abdominal pain) during steroid tapering in patients evaluated for cranial neuropathies.

title: A 35-Year-Old Woman with Subacute Bulbar Palsy, Right-Sided Lower Cranial Neuropathies, and Prior Corpus Callosal Stroke

presentation.chief_complaint: Subacute dysphagia, dysphonia, and nasal dysarthria
presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 3-month history of progressive dysphagia affecting liquids worse than solids, accompanied by coughing, nasal regurgitation, and a nasal quality to her voice. She had a history of a left-sided cerebral infarction 1 year prior involving the corpus callosum. She denied headaches, visual changes, seizures, or limb weakness, and her bulbar symptoms had stabilized without fatiguability.
presentation.past_medical_history: History of left cerebral infarction (corpus callosal involvement) 1 year prior; otherwise unremarkable.
presentation.neuro_exam: Alert and oriented. Cranial nerve examination revealed right upper motor neuron facial nerve palsy, deviation of the palate to the left, diminished right gag reflex, right tongue hemiatrophy with deviation to the right upon protrusion, and weak right sternocleidomastoid/trapezius contraction (Collet-Sicard syndrome, involving cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII). Motor examination showed mild right upper motor neuron hemiparesis with an extensor plantar response on the right and flexor on the left.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein, with negative bacterial, fungal, and viral PCR panels, and negative cytology.

imaging.caption: Magnetic resonance imaging at the time of right hemiparesis. Infarctions (arrows) are seen as hyperintense lesions in the corpus callosum on DWI ( A ) and T2-weighted axial ( C ) and sagittal ( D ) images, with corresponding hypointensities on the ADC map B . MRA ( E , F ) demonstrates a focal stenosis in the right MCA (arrowhead in E). DWI, diffusion-weighted imaging; ADC, apparent diffusion coefficient; MRA, magnetic resonance angiography; MCA, middle cerebral artery
imaging.findings_summary: Demonstrates hyperintense corpus callosal infarctions on DWI/T2 with corresponding ADC hypointensities, alongside a focal stenosis in the right middle cerebral artery.

imaging.caption: Cerebral digital subtraction angiography. Panels A and B show anteroposterior views of the right and left anterior circulations, respectively, while panel C shows a sagittal view of the right anterior circulation. Insets 1 and 2 provide magnified views of the right pericallosal (PCA) and callosomarginal arteries (CMA), respectively. Panel A demonstrates focal narrowing of the right MCA (arrow). Irregular luminal narrowing is also noted in the right callosomarginal artery (inset 2) and pericallosal artery (inset 1). MCA, middle cerebral artery; ACA, anterior cerebral artery; CMA, calloso-margin
imaging.findings_summary: Revealed multifocal intracranial arterial stenoses and luminal irregularities in the right MCA, pericallosal, and callosomarginal arteries.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Incorrect. While glomus tumors can cause jugular foramen syndromes, contrast-enhanced CT and high-resolution MRI of the skull base were entirely normal with no bony erosion or mass.

Incorrect. Skull-base osteomyelitis typically presents with severe local pain, cranial neuropathies, and characteristic inflammatory or destructive changes on skull-base imaging, which were absent here.
Incorrect. Jugular vein thrombosis can involve the lower cranial nerves within the foramen, but neuroimaging specifically confirmed the absence of venous thrombosis or jugular foramen pathology.

options.text: Intracranial vasculitic arteriopathy with vasa nervorum involvement
options.rationale: Correct! The patient presents with Collet-Sicard syndrome (IX, X, XI, XII palsies) alongside prior unusual corpus callosal infarction and angiographic evidence of multifocal intracranial stenoses. With normal skull-base imaging excluding local structural compression, the lower cranial neuropathies are attributed to vasculitic involvement of the vasa nervorum in the setting of probable intracranial vasculitic arteriopathy.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Collet-Sicard syndrome secondary to probable intracranial vasculitic arteriopathy
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Collet-Sicard syndrome is characterized by the simultaneous involvement of cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII, typically localizing pathology to the jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal. Classical etiologies include neoplasms, trauma, and vascular lesions such as ICA dissections. However, when skull-base neuroimaging is entirely unrevealing, clinicians must consider non-structural or systemic processes. 

In this patient, the presence of a prior corpus callosal infarction at a young age coupled with digital subtraction angiography demonstrating multifocal intracranial stenoses and luminal irregularities strongly pointed toward an intracranial vasculopathy. Given the absence of systemic rheumatologic markers, primary central nervous system or intracranial vasculitis affecting the vasa nervorum of the lower cranial nerves represents the most coherent pathophysiological explanation for this rare presentation.
teaching_points: Collet-Sicard syndrome involves ipsilateral palsies of cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII, localizing to the jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal.

When structural skull-base pathologies (tumors, fractures, infections, venous thrombosis) are ruled out by high-resolution neuroimaging, alternative mechanisms such as vasculitic vasa nervorum infarction should be investigated.
Multifocal intracranial arterial stenoses and irregularities on digital subtraction angiography in young stroke patients should raise suspicion for intracranial vasculitic arteriopathy.
clinical_pitfalls: Failing to look beyond local structural lesions at the skull base when evaluating lower cranial neuropathies, thereby missing systemic or intracranial vascular etiologies.
Overlooking unusual stroke locations (such as corpus callosal infarcts) as potential clues to an underlying systemic or central nervous system vasculopathy.

title: Progressive Chorea, Orofacial Dystonia, and Cognitive Decline in a Young Adult

presentation.chief_complaint: Severe involuntary facial and limb movements, difficulty speaking, and progressive cognitive decline over 10 years.
presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with progressive generalized choreiform movements and severe lingual/orofacial dystonia that first began at age 27. Her family notes that her feeding dystonia and tongue protrusion are severe, though placing a folded towel in her mouth partially relieves the dystonic spasms, suggestive of a sensory trick. Over the past decade, she has experienced gradual cognitive decline and mood changes. Her older brother was independently evaluated for mild distal paresthesias and distal lower extremity weakness at age 32, later developing facial involuntary movements. Their parents are second cousins and neurologically unimpaired.
presentation.past_medical_history: Consanguineous parental lineage (first cousins once removed / second cousins). No other chronic medical conditions.
presentation.neuro_exam: Alert, attentive, but demonstrates moderate global cognitive impairment (MMSE 21/30). Cranial nerve examination reveals prominent dysarthria, frequent involuntary tongue protrusion, and severe orofacial dystonia during attempt at speech or swallowing. Continuous moderate-to-severe choreic movements are observed in the neck, trunk, and upper and lower extremities. Muscle tone is variable with distal lower extremity hyporeflexia and symmetric distal sensory loss to vibration and pinprick. Plantar responses are flexor bilaterally.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Serum creatine kinase: 480 U/L (elevated). Liver function tests: Mild elevation in AST and ALT. Peripheral blood smear: 8% acanthocytes documented on fresh wet preparation. Nerve conduction studies: Sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy with reduced compound muscle action potentials and sensory nerve action potentials in lower extremities.

imaging.modality: Brain MRI (Axial T2 & Coronal FLAIR) and Peripheral Blood Smear
imaging.caption: Brain MRI of the younger sister and peripheral blood smear of the older brother. A , B Brain MRI of the younger sister obtained in 2016, approximately 10 years after symptom onset, showing findings suggestive of mild caudate atrophy on axial T2-weighted and coronal FLAIR images. Quantitative volumetric analysis was unavailable. C Peripheral blood smear from the older brother showing acanthocytosis (5%). Acanthocytosis was also documented in the younger sister (8%), although her smear image was unavailable. Scale bar = 14 μm
imaging.findings_summary: Axial T2 and coronal FLAIR images demonstrate mild caudate head atrophy with secondary enlargement of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles, while peripheral blood smear confirms acanthocytosis.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Correct! The combination of generalized chorea, severe feeding orofacial dystonia with lingual involvement, sensory tricks (towel in mouth), distal axonal neuropathy, elevated CK, acanthocytosis on peripheral blood smear, caudate atrophy, and autosomal recessive inheritance (consanguinity) is characteristic of chorea-acanthocytosis caused by pathogenic variants in VPS13A.

Incorrect. While Huntington disease presents with chorea, cognitive decline, and caudate atrophy, it follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern (HTT CAG expansion) and is typically not associated with peripheral axonal neuropathy, elevated serum CK, or acanthocytosis on blood smear.

Incorrect. McLeod syndrome is an X-linked recessive neuroacanthocytosis disorder caused by mutations in the XK gene on the X chromosome. It affects males predominantly and is characterized by absent Kx antigen and weak Kell antigen expression on red blood cells, often accompanied by cardiomyopathy.

Incorrect. PKAN (PANK2 mutations) is an autosomal recessive neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA) disorder that classically presents in childhood with dystonia, spasticity, and the characteristic 'eye-of-the-tiger' sign on T2-weighted brain MRI (globus pallidus hyperintensity surrounded by hypointensity), rather than primary caudate atrophy and peripheral acanthocytosis.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Chorea-acanthocytosis (VPS13A disease)
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Chorea-acanthocytosis (ChAc) is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder belonging to the core neuroacanthocytosis syndromes, caused by loss-of-function or pathogenic variants in the VPS13A gene on chromosome 9q21. VPS13A encodes chorein, a protein involved in inter-organelle lipid transfer and intracellular membrane trafficking. The clinical spectrum is marked by adult-onset movement disorders (most commonly generalized chorea and severe feeding dystonia characterized by tongue protrusion and involuntary bite injuries), cognitive impairment, psychiatric features, peripheral sensorimotor axonal neuropathy, elevated serum creatine kinase levels, and acanthocytes on peripheral blood smear.

Phenotypic variability can be marked even among siblings carrying identical homozygous genetic variants. As illustrated in this family, entry points can range from hyperkinetic-dystonic dominated phenotypes to neuropathy-predominant presentations where distal sensory symptoms and hyporeflexia precede involuntary extrapyramidal movements by several years. Recognition of peripheral nerve involvement, sensory tricks (such as holding objects or towels in the mouth), elevated CK, and caudate atrophy on MRI should prompt peripheral blood smear evaluation and VPS13A genetic testing.
teaching_points: Chorea-acanthocytosis (VPS13A disease) is an autosomal recessive neuroacanthocytosis disorder characterized by chorea, feeding orofacial dystonia, cognitive/psychiatric changes, axonal polyneuropathy, and peripheral acanthocytosis.
Intrafamilial phenotypic heterogeneity can occur with VPS13A variants, ranging from early hyperkinetic-dystonic presentations to neuropathy-predominant onset.
Diagnostic workup should include fresh blood smears (to evaluate for acanthocytes), serum CK level, nerve conduction studies, brain MRI (caudate head atrophy), and VPS13A genetic sequencing.
clinical_pitfalls: Misdiagnosing VPS13A disease as Huntington disease due to overlapping chorea, dementia, and caudate atrophy without ordering a blood smear or checking serum CK levels.
Failing to perform fresh wet blood smears or repeating blood smears, as acanthocyte percentages can fluctuate and standard automated blood counts often miss subtle acanthocytosis.

title: Acute Neurological Deterioration Following Transradial Vertebral Artery Stenting

presentation.chief_complaint: Acute altered consciousness and right hemiplegia post-procedure
presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient underwent uncomplicated right transradial vertebral artery stenting for severe ostial stenosis. Ten minutes post-procedure, he experienced an acute coughing episode followed by altered consciousness, mixed aphasia, and sudden right hemiplegia with an NIHSS score escalation from 0 to 16.
presentation.past_medical_history: Hypertension, prior cerebral infarction (6 years prior) with baseline mRS 1, compliant with optimal medical therapy including aspirin and atorvastatin.
presentation.neuro_exam: Altered consciousness, mixed aphasia, unable to follow commands. Spontaneous movements present in left extremities; no withdrawal to painful stimuli on the right side.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Platelets, coagulation profile, and basic metabolic panel within normal limits.

imaging.caption: A Pre-admission CTA revealing severe stenosis at the bilateral VA origins. B Admission MRI: prior right frontoparietal and corona radiata infarcts exhibited central hypointensity with peripheral hyperintensity on Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR), consistent with encephalomalacia and perifocal gliosis. C , D The prior left cerebellar hemisphere infarct showed FLAIR hypointensity, representing encephalomalacia foci
imaging.findings_summary: CTA confirmed severe bilateral vertebral artery ostial stenosis; MRI revealed prior right frontoparietal, corona radiata, and left cerebellar infarcts now converted to encephalomalacia.

imaging.caption: Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) findings. A Pre-intervention severe right VA ostial stenosis (white arrow). B Post-stenting patent vessel lumen (white arrow). C Post-stent implantation, right VA intracranial angiography: no visualization of left PCA (blue arrow). D , E Acute left MCA M2 segment occlusion (red arrow); left PCA visualized via left posterior communicating artery (PCoA), consistent with complete fetal-type posterior cerebral artery (CFPCA) (blue arrow)
imaging.findings_summary: DSA demonstrated successful right VA stenting but acute occlusion of the left MCA M2 segment, while post-procedure CT revealed linear hyperdensities in left cerebral sulci consistent with contrast extravasation.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely etiology for this patient's acute neurological deterioration following vertebral artery stenting?

options.text: Acute intracranial hemorrhage from secondary rupture
options.rationale: Incorrect. Immediate postoperative CT showed linear hyperdensities representing contrast extravasation rather than parenchymal or subarachnoid hemorrhage.

options.text: Procedural iatrogenic thromboembolism to the contralateral anterior circulation
options.rationale: Correct! The acute onset of aphasia and right hemiplegia immediately following vertebral artery stenting, combined with angiography proving left MCA M2 occlusion, confirms an iatrogenic embolic stroke to the contralateral territory during catheter manipulation.

options.text: Hypertensive encephalopathy due to blood pressure surges
options.rationale: Incorrect. Blood pressure was well-controlled and focal neurological signs with a discrete M2 occlusion on angiography point directly to a thromboembolic vascular event.
Incorrect. The patient's symptoms (aphasia, right hemiplegia) localize to the left middle cerebral artery territory, not the vertebrobasilar system or prior infarct beds.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Iatrogenic left middle cerebral artery embolism secondary to vertebral artery stenting
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Periprocedural stroke is a rare but devastating complication of vertebral artery stenting. This case highlights a paradoxical embolic event affecting the contralateral anterior circulation during a posterior circulation endovascular intervention. Catheter manipulation within the aortic arch or subclavian-vertebral junction can dislodge atheromatous debris or thrombi, which may propagate into unaffected cerebral territories. Despite attempts at mechanical thrombectomy, severe vascular tortuosity can preclude successful recanalization, necessitating alternative management strategies such as glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors (tirofiban), dual antiplatelet therapy, and intensive supportive care.

Post-procedural neuroimaging is critical to differentiate true intracranial hemorrhage from contrast extravasation (CE), a benign phenomenon resulting from blood-brain barrier disruption or stagnant flow during angiography. Recognizing CE prevents unwarranted discontinuation of antiplatelet therapies and inappropriate emergent surgical interventions. Long-term management requires careful balancing of ischemic stroke recurrence prevention against hemorrhagic transformation risks, paired with early, comprehensive neurorehabilitation to optimize functional recovery.
teaching_points: Vertebral artery stenting carries a procedural risk of distal or cross-territory thromboembolism due to catheter manipulation in the aortic arch.
Postoperative CT linear sulcal hyperdensities often represent benign contrast extravasation rather than true hemorrhagic transformation.
Severe vascular tortuosity can limit the technical success of mechanical thrombectomy, requiring medical rescue strategies such as intra-arterial and intravenous tirofiban.
clinical_pitfalls: Mistaking contrast extravasation for acute intracranial hemorrhage on non-contrast head CT, which can lead to inappropriate cessation of necessary antiplatelet therapy.
Underestimating the risk of anterior circulation embolization during posterior circulation endovascular procedures.

title: Acute Bulbar Failure, Albuminocytological Dissociation, and Areflexia in an Immunocompetent Man

presentation.chief_complaint: Acute progressive bulbar dysfunction and respiratory failure
presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with acute bulbar symptoms including progressive difficulty swallowing, change in phonation, and drooling that worsened over days, ultimately requiring intubation due to declining lung function and inability to manage secretions. He had no fever, recent infection, travel history, or vaccinations. Initial evaluation for a suspected lower motor neuron neuropathy showed absent gag/cough reflexes, tongue atrophy without fasciculations, and areflexia, prompting treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin for presumptive Guillain-Barré syndrome.
presentation.past_medical_history: Hypertension and remote unprovoked pulmonary embolism
presentation.neuro_exam: Alert and cooperative. Cranial nerves: CN IX and X dysfunction with absent gag and cough reflexes; mild tongue atrophy (CN XII) without fasciculations; no ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, or facial weakness. Motor: normal muscle bulk and strength in limbs. Sensory: intact to all modalities. Coordination: normal. Reflexes: absent at triceps and ankles, hyporeflexia at biceps and knees.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Lumbar puncture showed albuminocytological dissociation with a markedly elevated protein of 9.8 g/L, nonerythroid cell count of 13 cells/µL (77% lymphocytes), and normal glucose ratio. CSF PCR subsequently returned positive for Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV). Autoimmune and paraneoplastic panels were negative.

imaging.modality: Brain MRI (Axial T2 and T2-FLAIR with gadolinium)
imaging.caption: Image A , Axial T2 MRI brain, 2-weeks after presentation, shows a small focus of hyperintense signal in the left dorsal aspect of the medulla oblongata (arrow). Image B , Axial T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) MRI brain with gadolinium shows correlated enhancement of the same area (arrows), with no cranial nerve enhancement
imaging.findings_summary: Axial T2 and FLAIR images show a focal hyperintense signal and corresponding gadolinium enhancement in the left dorsal aspect of the medulla oblongata.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Incorrect. Although albuminocytological dissociation and areflexia initially suggested Guillain-Barré syndrome, the lack of clinical improvement following IVIG, the positive CSF viral PCR, and MRI demonstration of a medullary parenchymal lesion point to central nervous system infection rather than a peripheral neuropathy.
Incorrect. While brainstem gliomas can cause progressive bulbar symptoms, the acute presentation, inflammatory CSF profile, and positive CSF VZV PCR rule out a primary glial neoplasm.

Correct! The patient presented with acute bulbar dysfunction and profound CSF protein elevation, initially mimicking Guillain-Barré syndrome. However, the identification of VZV in the CSF alongside T2-hyperintense, enhancing medullary lesions on brain MRI confirms the diagnosis of VZV rhombencephalitis.

Incorrect. Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis typically presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and encephalopathy, often associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies, which does not match this patient's presentation or positive VZV CSF PCR.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Varicella-Zoster Virus Rhombencephalitis masquerading as Guillain-Barré syndrome
resolution.clinical_discussion:
This case illustrates a rare and deceptive clinical presentation where a central nervous system infection masqueraded as a peripheral neuropathy. The patient initially presented with isolated bulbar weakness, areflexia, and profound albuminocytological dissociation (protein 9.8 g/L) on lumbar puncture, which strongly pointed toward a diagnosis of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), specifically a bulbar variant. Consequently, he was treated with standard intravenous immunoglobulin therapy without clinical benefit.

Further evaluation revealed cerebrospinal fluid positive for varicella-zoster virus (VZV), and neuroimaging demonstrated focal inflammation within the dorsal medulla oblongata, confirming rhombencephalitis. Rhombencephalitis affects the hindbrain (brainstem and cerebellum) and can present with lower cranial neuropathies and bulbar failure. This case highlights that severe CSF albuminocytological dissociation is not exclusively seen in peripheral neuropathies like GBS; central infections, particularly viral rhombencephalitis, can also produce marked protein elevation, leading to diagnostic pitfalls.
teaching_points: Varicella-zoster virus can cause rhombencephalitis presenting with acute bulbar palsy, mimicking lower cranial nerve Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Cerebrospinal fluid albuminocytological dissociation (profound protein elevation with minimal lymphocytic pleocytosis) can occur in central nervous system infections such as VZV rhombencephalitis.
Brainstem parenchymal lesions and focal cranial nerve root entry zone enhancement on MRI distinguish brainstem encephalitis from peripheral polyradiculoneuropathies.
clinical_pitfalls: Assuming that profound albuminocytological dissociation with areflexia exclusively indicates a peripheral neuropathy like Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Failing to perform comprehensive CSF viral PCR panels when central brainstem signs overlap with peripheral nervous system manifestations.

title: Stereotyped Sensory Spells and Sulcal Subarachnoid Blood in Severe Extracranial ICA Stenosis

presentation.chief_complaint: Repetitive right-sided sensory episodes and headache
presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with repetitive, stereotyped, 5-to-10-minute episodes of right facial and distal upper limb paresthesias occurring 5 to 10 times daily over the preceding 5 days, recently associated with headache and transient visual symptoms. Cranial imaging revealed multi-lobar left hemispheric convexity subarachnoid hemorrhages (cSAHs) along with acute ischemia in the left anterior watershed area, occurring in the setting of severe bilateral extracranial internal carotid artery stenosis.
presentation.past_medical_history: Treated hypertension, heavy smoking history, and family history of stroke.
presentation.neuro_exam: Alert and oriented, language intact. No cranial nerve deficits or focal motor weakness on admission. Sensory examination revealed no fixed deficits between spells.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Routine blood work and coagulopathies unremarkable; CSF analysis was not performed.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism underlying the recurrent transient focal neurological episodes (TFNEs) in this patient?

options.text: Embolization from a cardiac source leading to recurrent cardioembolic transient ischemic attacks
options.rationale: Incorrect. Cardiac workup and imaging findings do not support a cardioembolic source; the lesions are localized to watershed zones and associated with severe ipsilateral ICA disease.

options.text: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) causing thunderclap headache and cortical ischemia
options.rationale: Incorrect. Although RCVS can cause cSAH, angiography demonstrated severe atherosclerotic extracranial ICA stenosis rather than the classic segmental cerebral vasoconstrictions.

options.text: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) with atypical unilateral convexity bleeding
options.rationale: Incorrect. The clinical presentation lacks acute severe encephalopathy, seizures, and typical bilateral posterior parieto-occipital vasogenic edema of PRES.

options.text: Convexity subarachnoid hemorrhage (cSAH) triggering focal cortical irritation or spreading ischemia via fragile collateral recruitment from severe ICA stenosis
options.rationale: Correct! The recurrent stereotyped sensory TFNEs closely resemble 'amyloid spells' or focal epileptic/irritative phenomena triggered by convexity subarachnoid hemorrhage resulting from fragile leptomeningeal collaterals recruited due to severe ipsilateral ICA stenosis.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Convexity subarachnoid hemorrhage (cSAH) and transient focal neurological episodes (TFNEs) secondary to severe ipsilateral internal carotid artery stenosis
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Spontaneous non-traumatic convexity subarachnoid hemorrhage (cSAH) accounts for approximately 5-10% of all subarachnoid hemorrhages and is frequently underdiagnosed. Unlike aneurysmal SAH, bleeding in cSAH is restricted to the cerebral sulci and does not extend to the basal cisterns. While RCVS and PRES are common etiologies in younger cohorts, severe atherosclerotic extracranial internal carotid artery (ICA) stenosis can occasionally lead to cSAH via the rupture of fragile, maximally recruited leptomeningeal collaterals—a mechanism analogous to hemodynamic stress seen in Moyamoya syndrome.

Patients with cSAH often present with transient focal neurological episodes (TFNEs) characterized by repetitive, stereotyped sensory or motor deficits that mimic transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) or focal seizures. In cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), similar episodes are termed 'amyloid spells' and are thought to result from superficial cortical hemosiderosis or recurrent micro-subarachnoid bleeding irritating the overlying cortex. Management requires careful balancing of secondary stroke prevention, hemodynamic optimization, and seizure control until definitive revascularization can be safely achieved.
teaching_points: Convexity subarachnoid hemorrhage (cSAH) is defined by sulcal blood restricted to the convexal surface without extension into the basal cisterns.
Severe extracranial ICA stenosis can precipitate cSAH by placing extreme hemodynamic stress on fragile leptomeningeal collaterals.
Transient focal neurological episodes (TFNEs) associated with cSAH can present as stereotyped sensory or motor spells mimicking TIAs or focal seizures ('amyloid-like spells').
Multimodal imaging including SWI/GRE MRI is essential to accurately detect sulcal subarachnoid blood products.
clinical_pitfalls: Mistaking cSAH-associated TFNEs purely for standard ischemic TIAs and omitting advanced neuroimaging (such as SWI) to evaluate for sulcal blood.
Overlooking severe extracranial or intracranial steno-occlusive disease as a structural cause of non-traumatic cSAH in younger or middle-aged adults.

title: Rapidly Progressive Early-Onset Memory Impairment with Familial Aggregation

presentation.chief_complaint: Progressive memory decline and occupational errors starting at age 47
presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient began exhibiting frequent occupational errors at age 47, including missed appointments and episodes of disorientation while driving. His memory impairment progressively worsened over eight months, leading him to present to the hospital. He has a strong family history of early-onset dementia: his older brother developed memory impairment at 47 and died at 55, his mother developed dementia starting at 65, and his maternal grandmother had significant forgetfulness.
presentation.past_medical_history: Hypertension diagnosed at age 42, untreated.
presentation.neuro_exam: Mini-Mental State Examination score of 20/30 with predominant disorientation and recent memory deficits. No other focal neurological abnormalities or extrapyramidal signs identified.
presentation.key_labs_csf: CSF analysis showed normal cell counts, protein, and glucose. Whole-exome sequencing revealed no mutations in APP, PSEN1, or PSEN2, but identified APOE epsilon4/epsilon4 homozygosity and the PRNP-V180I variant.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease with APOE epsilon4 homozygosity and PRNP-V180I variant
options.rationale: Correct! The patient's clinical presentation, CSF biomarker profile (low Abeta42/40 ratio and high p-tau), and neuroimaging findings of parietal and hippocampal atrophy are characteristic of early-onset Alzheimer's disease, significantly modulated by APOE epsilon4 homozygosity and the incidental or modifying PRNP-V180I variant.

Incorrect. Although the PRNP-V180I variant is associated with genetic prion disease, the patient lacks typical DWI hyperintensities, has an indolent 8-month progressive course with prominent hippocampal/parietal atrophy rather than rapid akinetic mutism, and has a CSF profile and APOE genotype highly specific for Alzheimer's disease.

options.text: Autosomal dominant early-onset Alzheimer's disease due to a PSEN1 mutation
options.rationale: Incorrect. While the patient has an autosomal dominant-appearing family history of early-onset dementia, whole-exome sequencing specifically confirmed the absence of pathogenic variants in APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2.

options.text: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration with behavioral variant
options.rationale: Incorrect. The clinical syndrome is characterized by prominent amnestic deficits, disorientation, and parietal-hippocampal atrophy with CSF biomarker confirmation of amyloid and tau pathology, rather than primary behavioral or executive dysfunction characteristic of frontotemporal dementia.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease with APOE epsilon4 homozygosity and PRNP-V180I variant
resolution.clinical_discussion:
This case highlights an unusual presentation of early-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD) in a 47-year-old male with a strong family history of dementia. Despite the striking autosomal dominant-like pedigree, genetic testing revealed no mutations in classical early-onset AD genes (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2). Instead, the patient was found to be homozygous for the APOE epsilon4 allele and carried the PRNP-V180I variant. APOE epsilon4 homozygosity is a well-established potent risk factor that dramatically lowers the age of onset and accelerates amyloid deposition, likely driving the familial aggregation seen in this pedigree.

The identification of the PRNP-V180I variant adds complexity, as V180I is typically associated with a genetic form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) characterized by late onset, slow progression, and characteristic cortical/basal ganglia DWI hyperintensities. However, the patient's CSF profile (low Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio and markedly elevated p-tau), typical AD neuroimaging pattern of parietal and hippocampal atrophy, and lack of restricted diffusion on DWI confirmed that the underlying pathology was AD. The coexistence of genetic risk variants underscores the challenges in diagnosing early-onset dementias and emphasizes the importance of comprehensive biomarker and genetic evaluations.
teaching_points: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease can present with a strong family history mimicking autosomal dominant inheritance without mutations in APP, PSEN1, or PSEN2.
APOE epsilon4 homozygosity significantly accelerates the age of onset and increases the risk of familial clustering in Alzheimer's disease.
The PRNP-V180I variant, typically linked to genetic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, can occasionally be identified in patients whose primary clinical and biomarker profile conforms to Alzheimer's disease.
CSF amyloid-beta and phosphorylated tau assays are critical biomarkers to differentiate AD pathology from prion diseases when clinical presentations overlap.
clinical_pitfalls: Assuming a patient with a strong autosomal dominant family history of early-onset dementia automatically harbors a pathogenic APP, PSEN1, or PSEN2 mutation.
Mistaking incidental or co-occurring genetic variants (such as PRNP variants) for the primary cause of rapidly progressive dementia without corroborating neuroimaging and CSF biomarker support.

title: Fulminant Refractory Cerebral Encephalopathy with Rapidly Progressive Vasogenic Edema and Microhemorrhages

presentation.chief_complaint: Seizure, progressive left hemiparesis, and acute neurological decline
presentation.history_of_present_illness: A 70-year-old woman presented with a seizure characterized by left hemiparesis, followed by loss of consciousness, bladder incontinence, and right gaze preference. For weeks prior, she exhibited unintentional weight loss and malaise. Initial brain MRI showed multifocal subcortical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities with cortical microhemorrhages without gadolinium enhancement. Despite initial high-dose steroid therapy and an outpatient taper, she developed worsening focal deficits, severe headache, and nausea. She represented with marked clinical decline, and repeat imaging revealed severe vasogenic edema with subfalcine and uncal herniation refractory to high-dose corticosteroids, hyperosmolar therapy, and cyclophosphamide.
presentation.past_medical_history: Hypertension
presentation.neuro_exam: Lethargic, oriented only to self. Right pupil dilated (5 mm) and sluggishly reactive; left pupil 3 mm and reactive. Right gaze preference noted. Dense left-sided hemiplegia with hyperreflexia and a left extensor plantar response.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 88 mm/h, C-reactive protein 4.4 mg/L, white blood cell count 12.99 K/uL.

imaging.findings_summary: Asymmetric multifocal subcortical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities with associated cortical microhemorrhages on susceptibility-weighted imaging, progressing to massive vasogenic edema and midline shift.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely pathological diagnosis?

options.text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS)
options.rationale: Incorrect. PACNS displays transmural lymphocytic or granulomatous vasculitis on brain biopsy, but it lacks the characteristic vascular amyloid deposition (Congo red positivity with apple-green birefringence) that defines amyloid beta-related angiitis.

Correct! The combination of subacute encephalopathy, prominent lobar microhemorrhages, extensive vasogenic edema, and histopathology revealing vessel-centric granulomatous inflammation (multinucleated giant cells) directly targeting amyloid-laden cortical/leptomeningeal vessels confirms amyloid beta-related angiitis.
Incorrect. Neurosarcoidosis typically demonstrates non-caseating granulomatous inflammation in a non-vasculitic perivascular or leptomeningeal distribution, without vascular amyloid deposition.

Incorrect. PCNSL histopathology demonstrates atypical, highly mitotic neoplastic lymphocytes forming tight angiocentric cuffs, lacking granulomatous giant cell infiltrates and vascular amyloid deposits.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Amyloid Beta-Related Angiitis (ABRA)
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Amyloid beta-related angiitis (ABRA) is a rare, severe subtype of cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related inflammation (CAA-ri) characterized by an autoimmune inflammatory response directed against beta-amyloid peptides deposited in the walls of leptomeningeal and cortical blood vessels. Patients typically present with rapidly progressive cognitive decline, seizures, focal neurological deficits, and headaches. Neuroimaging is critical, demonstrating asymmetric subcortical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities, extensive vasogenic edema, and a high burden of lobar microhemorrhages or superficial siderosis on susceptibility-weighted sequences. Definite diagnosis requires brain biopsy showing transmural or perivascular infiltration by lymphocytes, epithelioid macrophages, and multinucleated giant cells surrounding amyloid-laden vessels (Congo red positive with apple-green birefringence).

Management of fulminant ABRA can be exceptionally challenging, frequently requiring high-dose corticosteroids, cytotoxic agents like cyclophosphamide, and aggressive neuro-intensive care measures for intracranial hypertension and herniation. In refractory cases, targeted biological therapies such as tocilizumab (an anti-interleukin-6 receptor monoclonal antibody) offer a promising alternative by interrupting the inflammatory cascade and mitigating the need for decompressive hemicraniectomy. Rapid clinical and radiological improvement following IL-6 blockade highlights the prominent role of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the pathogenesis of refractory ABRA.
teaching_points: Amyloid beta-related angiitis (ABRA) is a distinct, inflammatory subtype of cerebral amyloid angiopathy presenting with subacute encephalopathy, seizures, and focal deficits.
MRI findings classically include asymmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensities, prominent vasogenic edema, and numerous lobar microhemorrhages on susceptibility-weighted imaging.
Definite diagnosis relies on brain biopsy demonstrating granulomatous or lymphocytic vessel wall inflammation targeting amyloid-beta-laden cortical and leptomeningeal vessels.
Refractory fulminant cases failing high-dose corticosteroids and cytotoxic chemotherapy can achieve dramatic clinical and radiological responses with targeted anti-IL-6 therapy (tocilizumab).
clinical_pitfalls: Mistaking the extensive vasogenic edema of ABRA for a malignant infiltrative glioma or primary CNS lymphoma, leading to delayed or inappropriate therapies.
Failing to recognize that standard steroid tapers can trigger rapid clinical relapses and life-threatening intracranial herniation in severe CAA-ri and ABRA.

title: Recurrent Seizures and Symmetric Occipital Cortico-Subcortical Lesions in an Infant

presentation.chief_complaint: Recurrent afebrile generalized tonic-clonic seizures
presentation.history_of_present_illness: A previously healthy 4-month-old infant presents with acute onset of recurrent spontaneous generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Between episodes, the infant demonstrates prompt postictal recovery and preserved responsiveness. Despite receiving intravenous midazolam and phenobarbital, the infant experiences breakthrough convulsions requiring admission to the pediatric intensive care unit for airway protection and seizure management.
presentation.past_medical_history: Unremarkable. Born full-term via uncomplicated vaginal delivery with normal baseline growth and development.
presentation.neuro_exam: Interactive and alert between seizure episodes. Age-appropriate cranial nerve exam with normal pupillary responses. Normal, symmetric tone and deep tendon reflexes throughout. No focal motor deficits or meningeal signs.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Serum glucose: 98 mg/dL (5.4 mmol/L). Serum electrolytes, renal function, liver function, serum ammonia, and lactate are within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrates normal cell count, glucose, and protein with negative PCR testing.

imaging.caption: Axial brain CT scan revealing no parenchymal lesions or extra-axial collections
imaging.findings_summary: Initial axial cranial CT scan revealed no parenchymal lesions, acute hemorrhage, or extra-axial collections.

imaging.caption: MRI identified a cortico-subcortical signal abnormality in the occipital lobes (thin arrows), bilaterally distributed with close symmetry. The lesions appear hyperintense on FLAIR ( A ) and diffusion-weighted imaging ( B ), with corresponding mildly reduced ADC signal on the ADC map ( C ). Overall, these findings are suggestive of PRES, predominantly vasogenic in pattern, with a possible superimposed cytotoxic component
imaging.findings_summary: Bilateral, symmetrical cortico-subcortical occipital hyperintensities on FLAIR and DWI with mildly reduced ADC signal, indicative of vasogenic edema with a possible superimposed cytotoxic component.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Incorrect. Herpes simplex encephalitis characteristically presents with fever, focal temporal lobe involvement, CSF pleocytosis, and cytotoxic edema, none of which are present in this afebrile infant with symmetric posterior vasogenic edema.

Incorrect. Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy typically follows a documented perinatal or systemic hypoxic-ischemic insult and preferentially affects deep gray matter structures (basal ganglia/thalami) or vascular watershed regions, with marked cytotoxic edema (diffusion restriction).

Correct! Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) presents with acute neurological symptoms (such as seizures and altered mental status) and neuroimaging showing bilateral, symmetrical parieto-occipital subcortical vasogenic edema (facilitated diffusion on ADC maps). Elevated blood pressure for age (104/68 mmHg is significantly above the 99th percentile for a 4-month-old) further supports this diagnosis.

Incorrect. X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy typically manifests in early childhood (ages 4–8 years) with progressive neurodevelopmental decline and symmetrical confluent parieto-occipital white matter demyelination, rather than acute seizure onset in a 4-month-old infant.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES)
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is a clinico-radiological entity characterized by acute neurological signs—most commonly seizures, altered mental status, and visual disturbances—in setting of characteristic neuroimaging features. The pathophysiological hallmark of PRES is failure of cerebral autoregulation and endothelial dysfunction leading to vasogenic edema, predominantly involving the posterior parieto-occipital subcortical white matter.

While PRES is well recognized in adults and older children with severe hypertension, renal disease, or chemotherapy exposure, it is under-recognized in early infancy. Normal blood pressure values in infants are considerably lower than in adults; a blood pressure of 104/68 mmHg in a 4-month-old infant represents stage 2 hypertension (>99th percentile + 5 mmHg), which can trigger cerebral hyperperfusion and PRES. Cranial CT is frequently unrevealing in early stages. Brain MRI is essential, demonstrating hyperintense signal on T2/FLAIR with high ADC values indicating vasogenic rather than cytotoxic edema. Early recognition, acute blood pressure management, and anti-seizure therapy lead to clinical and radiological recovery in the majority of cases.
teaching_points: Blood pressure norms in infants are age-dependent; a BP of 104/68 mmHg in a 4-month-old infant is significantly elevated (>99th percentile) and sufficient to trigger PRES.
MRI with DWI/ADC mapping is crucial to differentiate vasogenic edema (characteristic of PRES, showing high ADC values) from cytotoxic edema (stroke or infection, showing ADC restriction).
Initial non-contrast cranial CT in infants with PRES can be normal, so MRI should be obtained promptly when clinical suspicion is high.
clinical_pitfalls: Misinterpreting infant blood pressure readings using adult reference ranges, thereby missing pediatric stage 2 hypertension as a cause of PRES.
Assuming normal cranial CT rules out structural or vascular acute brain pathology in infants presenting with new-onset status epilepticus.

title: Progressive Numbness, Gait Instability, and Posterior Cervical Cord T2 Hyperintensity in a Young Adult

presentation.chief_complaint: Progressive numbness of limbs and unsteady gait for 3 months
presentation.history_of_present_illness: A 23-year-old female presents with a 3-month history of progressive limb numbness and gait instability, which worsened significantly over the 2 weeks prior to evaluation. She reports inhaling nitrous oxide (N₂O) via whipped cream chargers 3 to 4 times weekly (10–15 cartridges per session) for the past 6 months. She admits to unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple partners over the preceding year, but denies primary genital lesions, rash, fever, or systemic symptoms.
presentation.past_medical_history: Unremarkable. No prior gastrointestinal disease, bariatric surgery, chronic malabsorption, or blood transfusions.
presentation.neuro_exam: Cranial nerves are normal. Muscle tone is decreased in both lower extremities. Muscle strength is 4/5 in proximal and distal lower extremities and 5/5 in upper extremities. Reduced vibration and joint position sensation below the iliac crests, with stocking-glove hypoesthesia to pinprick. Patellar and Achilles reflexes are absent bilaterally; upper extremity reflexes are 1+. Romberg sign is positive. Impaired heel-to-shin testing bilaterally. Meningeal signs are negative.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Isolated nitrous oxide-induced subacute combined degeneration
options.rationale: Incorrect. While nitrous oxide abuse and vitamin B12 deficiency account for the myelopathy and spinal MRI findings, ignoring the reactive CSF TPPA and TRUST fails to recognize concurrent neurosyphilis.

Incorrect. Although CSF serology confirms neurosyphilis, neurosyphilis alone does not account for the severe vitamin B12 deficiency and elevated homocysteine precipitated by recreational nitrous oxide inhalation.

Incorrect. Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by GAA repeat expansions in the FXN gene. It typically presents in childhood or adolescence with slowly progressive ataxia, loss of deep tendon reflexes, skeletal abnormalities, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, rather than subacute adult-onset myelopathy with metabolic and treponemal abnormalities.

options.text: Nitrous oxide-induced subacute combined degeneration with concurrent neurosyphilis
options.rationale: Correct! The patient presents with a classic history of nitrous oxide abuse leading to functional vitamin B12 inactivation and subacute combined degeneration (evidenced by the spinal 'inverted V-sign' and severe B12 deficiency), alongside concurrently confirmed neurosyphilis (reactive CSF TPPA and TRUST). Recognizing dual pathologies is essential for comprehensive treatment with both vitamin B12 repletion and high-dose IV penicillin.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Nitrous oxide-induced subacute combined degeneration with concurrent neurosyphilis
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Subacute combined degeneration (SCD) is caused by vitamin B12 deficiency, which can be acutely precipitated by nitrous oxide (N₂O) abuse. Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidizes the cobalt moiety of cobalamin, inactivating methionine synthase. This impairs myelin sheath maintenance and leads to symmetric demyelination of the posterior and lateral columns of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord, classically producing an 'inverted V-sign' on axial T2-weighted MRI.

Simultaneously, Treponema pallidum invasion of the central nervous system leads to neurosyphilis. In rare cases, spinal neurosyphilis (such as tabes dorsalis or syphilitic meningomyelitis) can involve the dorsal columns and clinically resemble SCD. When young patients present with atypical or multi-factorial clinical features, comprehensive laboratory evaluations—including infectious, autoimmune, and metabolic panels—are necessary to avoid single-etiology diagnostic bias and ensure appropriate multi-modal therapy.
teaching_points: Nitrous oxide oxidizes cobalamin (vitamin B12), inactivating methionine synthase and precipitating subacute combined degeneration.
The 'inverted V-sign' on axial T2-weighted spinal MRI represents selective demyelination of the posterior columns.
Neurosyphilis can coexist with metabolic or substance-induced myelopathies and requires dedicated serologic and CSF confirmation.
Comprehensive diagnostic screening prevents missed comorbid diagnoses that require independent therapeutic regimens (e.g., parenteral penicillin and intramuscular cobalamin).
clinical_pitfalls: Attributing spinal cord pathology exclusively to a history of substance abuse while omitting routine infectious and autoimmune workups.
Failing to perform lumbar puncture in sexually active patients presenting with unexplained neuro-axial symptoms or atypical diagnostic findings.

title: Super-Refractory Status Epilepticus and Parieto-Occipital Restriction in a Young Adult with Baseline Optic Atrophy and Ataxia
author_credit: Annals of clinical and translational neurology • PMC13393509

source_journal.name: Annals of clinical and translational neurology
source_journal.short_name: Annals of clinical and translational neurology

presentation.chief_complaint: New-onset super-refractory status epilepticus
presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with sudden-onset status epilepticus characterized by occipital-predominant epileptiform activity and continuous seizure activity refractory to multiple lines of antiepileptic drugs and anesthetic infusions. Despite a lifelong neurodegenerative phenotype including generalized hypotonia, celiac disease, legal blindness from optic atrophy, cerebellar ataxia, and progressive motor decline, she had no prior history of clinical seizures. Brain MRI revealed transient diffusion restriction in the right parieto-occipital cortex and cerebellum, mimicking an acute ischemic stroke or mitochondrial encephalopathy.
presentation.past_medical_history: Optic atrophy with legal blindness, cerebellar ataxia, generalized hypotonia, progressive motor decline, and celiac disease, without prior history of seizures.
presentation.neuro_exam: Comatose under general anesthesia (propofol/midazolam burst-suppression). Baseline interictal examination prior to intubation demonstrated optic atrophy with visual loss, generalized hypotonia, absent deep tendon reflexes, and severe limb and truncal ataxia.
presentation.key_labs_csf: CSF analysis unremarkable for infectious or autoimmune etiologies. Comprehensive autoimmune encephalitis panel negative. Lactate mildly elevated. Genetic panel revealed compound heterozygous variants in the OPA1 gene (frameshift p.Val903GlyfsTer3 and missense p.Ile382Met).

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely underlying genetic etiology for this patient's super-refractory status epilepticus?

options.text: Compound heterozygous OPA1 variants causing mitochondrial dynamics dysfunction
options.rationale: Correct! The patient harbors compound heterozygous OPA1 variants (frameshift and missense in the GTPase domain) disrupting mitochondrial fusion. In severe biallelic loss-of-function, secondary metabolic stressors can trigger a diffuse energy crisis and catastrophic super-refractory status epilepticus.

options.text: POLG mutations causing mitochondrial DNA depletion and respiratory chain failure
options.rationale: Incorrect. While POLG mutations commonly present with status epilepticus and stroke-like lesions, POLG typically causes severe mtDNA depletion and respiratory chain failure, whereas OPA1 dysfunction disrupts mitochondrial inner membrane fusion while largely sparing baseline mtDNA copy number.

options.text: MT-TL1 m.3243A>G mutation causing MELAS syndrome
options.rationale: Incorrect. MELAS classically presents with stroke-like episodes, lactic acidosis, and seizures due to mitochondrial tRNA leucine mutations, which does not match the specific OPA1 compound heterozygous genotype and baseline optic atrophy phenotype.

Incorrect. Although autoimmune encephalitis is a primary consideration in unexplained super-refractory status epilepticus, the patient's negative autoimmune panels, longstanding baseline neurodegenerative disorder, and genetic testing confirm a genetic mitochondrial etiology.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Mitochondrial Super-Refractory Status Epilepticus (SRSE) secondary to OPA1 variants
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Super-Refractory Status Epilepticus (SRSE) with unclear etiology remains one of the most formidable emergencies in neurocritical care. When standard anticonvulsants and anesthetics fail and infectious or structural triggers are absent, clinicians frequently suspect autoimmune or parainfectious etiologies, prompting aggressive broad-spectrum immunosuppressive therapies. However, as demonstrated in this case, underlying primary mitochondrial and energy metabolism defects can manifest as catastrophic SRSE without prior history of epilepsy. 

This patient presented with mitochondrial-associated SRSE caused by compound heterozygous OPA1 gene variants (p.Val903GlyfsTer3 and p.Ile382Met) affecting the GTPase domain. Unlike POLG or MELAS-related epilepsies driven by mtDNA depletion or primary respiratory chain failure, OPA1 dysfunction primarily impairs mitochondrial inner membrane fusion and network dynamics. In the setting of severe biallelic loss-of-function, physiological stressors can precipitate a catastrophic neuronal energy crisis, resulting in refractory status epilepticus and cortical diffusion restriction mimicking acute ischemia or stroke-like episodes. Recognizing these genetic underpinnings prevents inappropriate exposure to potentially harmful immunosuppressive regimens and highlights the diagnostic utility of comprehensive genetic testing in unexplained SRSE.
teaching_points: Unexplained super-refractory status epilepticus (SRSE) in young patients should prompt consideration of underlying mitochondrial and energy metabolism defects.

OPA1 gene variants, typically associated with autosomal dominant optic atrophy, can present with severe biallelic loss-of-function phenotypes including cerebellar ataxia, motor decline, and catastrophic SRSE.
Unlike POLG and MELAS which feature mtDNA depletion and respiratory chain failure, OPA1 dysfunction disrupts mitochondrial fusion dynamics and can trigger energy-crisis mediated seizures.
clinical_pitfalls: Assuming all cryptogenic SRSE cases are autoimmune and reflexively exposing patients to toxic broad-spectrum immunosuppression without genetic screening.

Overlooking mitochondrial disorders in patients presenting with status epilepticus who lack a prior personal history of epilepsy but possess chronic neurological symptoms like optic atrophy or ataxia.

title: Subacute Myelopathy and Visual Loss with Normal Spinal MRI

presentation.chief_complaint: Progressive lower limb weakness and urinary urgency
presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a subacute onset of visual loss followed by urinary urgency and insidious lower limb weakness. Neurological examination revealed a T11 sensory level, lower limb weakness, and diffuse hyperreflexia. Spinal MRI performed 2 months after symptom onset was unremarkable, while subsequent 18F-FDG PET-CT demonstrated spinal cord hypermetabolism at the T11 level.
presentation.past_medical_history: Unremarkable
presentation.neuro_exam: Visual acuity reduced bilaterally; T11 sensory level; lower extremity weakness (4/5); diffuse hyperreflexia; urodynamic testing confirms detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Serum ACE: 387 U/L (High); CSF: 6 WBC/mm3; Anti-MOG and Anti-AQP4: Negative.

imaging.caption: The line marks the T11 level (C), demonstrating spinal cord hypermetabolism (SUVmax 2.0, arrowhead [F]) with normal MRI corresponding images. 18 F-FDG = 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose; SUVmax = maximum standardized uptake value.
imaging.findings_summary: Focal hypermetabolism (SUVmax 2.0) at the T11 spinal cord level despite a normal corresponding spinal MRI.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Incorrect. While NMOSD can present with optic neuritis and myelitis, the patient tested negative for AQP4 antibodies and the clinical picture of systemic lymphadenopathy and elevated ACE is more specific for sarcoidosis.

Correct! The combination of granulomatous uveitis, elevated serum ACE, systemic lymphadenopathy, and spinal cord hypermetabolism on PET-CT in the setting of clinical myelitis is highly suggestive of neurosarcoidosis.
Incorrect. MS typically presents with characteristic T2-hyperintense lesions on MRI; a normal spinal MRI 2 months into symptomatic myelitis makes MS unlikely.
Incorrect. Spinal cord infarction presents with acute, rather than subacute, onset and would typically show restricted diffusion on MRI, not hypermetabolism on PET.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis
resolution.clinical_discussion:
This case illustrates the diagnostic challenge of MRI-negative myelitis in the context of neurosarcoidosis. While MRI is the gold standard for spinal imaging, inflammatory activity can occasionally be occult on structural sequences, particularly in early or infiltrative stages of granulomatous disease. The use of 18F-FDG PET-CT serves as a powerful adjunct, revealing metabolic activity that correlates with clinical symptoms.

The diagnosis of neurosarcoidosis in this patient was supported by the systemic findings of noncaseating granulomas on biopsy, elevated serum ACE, and granulomatous uveitis. The presence of detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia confirms the spinal cord involvement, despite the lack of structural changes on conventional T1 and T2-weighted MRI sequences.
teaching_points: Neurosarcoidosis can present with clinical myelitis even when conventional spinal MRI is normal.
18F-FDG PET-CT is a sensitive modality for detecting occult spinal cord inflammation in neurosarcoidosis.
Systemic signs such as elevated ACE, lymphadenopathy, and uveitis are critical clues for diagnosing neurosarcoidosis in patients with unexplained neurological deficits.
clinical_pitfalls: Assuming a normal spinal MRI rules out inflammatory myelitis.
Over-reliance on MRI without considering metabolic imaging in patients with high clinical suspicion for systemic inflammatory disease.

title: Bilateral Visual Disturbance and Hypertension in a Young Adult

presentation.chief_complaint: Bilateral blurred vision
presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a half-month history of progressive bilateral blurred vision, more prominent during near tasks, and left-eye predominance, without visual field defects. Upon admission, he was found to have severe malignant hypertension with a blood pressure of 200/132 mmHg. Neurological examination showed bilateral decreased visual acuity (0.8 OD, 0.4 OS) but was otherwise completely unremarkable with no focal motor, sensory, or coordination deficits.
presentation.past_medical_history: No previous history of cardiocerebrovascular diseases; newly uncovered malignant hypertension with concurrent mixed glomerular and tubular renal injury.
presentation.neuro_exam: Alert and oriented. Cranial nerves: Bilateral decrease in visual acuity (OD 0.8, OS 0.4); remaining cranial nerves intact. Motor: Normal muscle strength and tone throughout. Sensory: Intact to all modalities. Reflexes: Normal symmetrical tendon reflexes, no pathological signs. Coordination: Finger-nose and heel-knee-shin tests normal.

challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Incorrect. While NMOSD can involve the optic nerve and spinal cord, the acute malignant hypertension and prompt complete imaging and clinical resolution with blood pressure control alone exclude an inflammatory demyelinating disorder.
Incorrect. Bilateral PCA infarctions typically present with permanent visual field cuts and show restricted diffusion on DWI rather than completely reversible vasogenic edema.

options.text: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome with spinal cord involvement (PRES-SCI)
options.rationale: Correct. The acute presentation of blurred vision in the setting of malignant hypertension, combined with simultaneous, fully reversible T2-FLAIR hyperintense vasogenic edema involving the supratentorial region, infratentorial structures, and the cervical spinal cord, confirms PRES-SCI.

Incorrect. ADEM typically presents following an infection or vaccination with a monophasic demyelinating encephalopathy showing multifocal white matter lesions that require immunotherapy rather than rapid resolution strictly via blood pressure management.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome with spinal cord involvement (PRES-SCI)
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is a clinical-neuroradiological entity characterized by headache, encephalopathy, seizures, and visual disturbances, driven by acute blood pressure dysregulation or endothelial injury. While classically restricted to the posterior parieto-occipital cerebral white matter, atypical variants can involve the frontal lobes, basal ganglia, brainstem, cerebellum, and extremely rarely, the spinal cord (PRES-SCI). Spinal cord involvement typically extends from the cervicomedullary junction and can mimic myelitis or spinal cord ischemia.

Prompt identification of the underlying etiology—most frequently malignant hypertension, eclampsia, or cytotoxic agents—is critical. In PRES-SCI, neuroimaging demonstrates characteristic long T1, long T2, and FLAIR hyperintensities representing vasogenic edema without cytotoxic infarction on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). With timely and aggressive blood pressure regulation, the clinical deficits and radiological lesions are remarkably reversible, yielding an exceptionally favorable prognosis as demonstrated in this case.
teaching_points: PRES-SCI is an extremely rare variant of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome where vasogenic edema extends beyond the brain into the cervical spinal cord.
Malignant hypertension is a primary precipitating trigger, disrupting cerebral and spinal autoregulatory thresholds and leading to endothelial breakdown.
Radiologically, lesions manifest as T2/FLAIR hyperintensities with facilitated diffusion on ADC/DWI, distinguishing vasogenic from cytotoxic edema.
Prompt blood pressure control leads to rapid and complete radiological and clinical resolution.
clinical_pitfalls: Failing to consider PRES when spinal cord signs or brainstem lesions accompany visual disturbances, leading to misdiagnosis as transverse myelitis or demyelinating disease.
Delaying aggressive antihypertensive therapy while waiting for extensive autoimmune or infectious workups in a patient with malignant hypertension-induced PRES.

title: Fever, Seizures, and Multifocal Brain Lesions Without Cutaneous Manifestations in an Older Adult

presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with acute onset of high fever, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and rapidly progressive impairment of consciousness. He had no history of recent trauma, vaccinations, or noticeable skin eruptions, vesicles, or localized rashes across his body. Initial evaluation showed marked neurological decline requiring urgent neuroimaging and cerebrospinal fluid analysis.

presentation.neuro_exam: Drowsy, confused, unable to fully cooperate with cognitive testing. Cranial nerves intact without focal deficits. Generalized hyperreflexia; no meningeal signs present. No cutaneous lesions or dermatomal scarring observed.
presentation.key_labs_csf: CSF opening pressure normal. CSF analysis demonstrated marked pleocytosis, elevated protein levels, and cytology revealing suspected atypical lymphocytes. CSF metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) sequences.
