challenge.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Incorrect. Classic biphasic encephalitis typically emerges weeks to months after the initial viral infection rather than presenting concurrently within the first 72 hours.
Incorrect. While viral pathogens are detected, the simultaneous presence of neuronal autoantibodies indicates an immune-mediated co-pathology rather than isolated viral destruction.

options.text: Primary psychiatric disorder with incidental viral shedding
options.rationale: Incorrect. The acute inflammatory CSF profile, MRI abnormalities, and documented autoantibodies rule out a primary psychiatric etiology.

Correct! Overlapping Peak Encephalitis (OPE) is defined by the concomitant detection of viral CNS infection and neuronal autoantibodies within a narrow 72-hour window from symptom onset, representing a distinct clinical entity from delayed biphasic autoimmune encephalitis.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Overlapping Peak Encephalitis (OPE) / Coincidence Condition
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Overlapping Peak Encephalitis (OPE), also conceptualized as a coincidence condition, is defined by the concomitant detection of evidence of viral CNS infection (via mNGS) and neuronal autoantibodies (via cytometric bead array) within 72 hours of symptom onset. This distinguishes OPE from traditional biphasic encephalitis, where autoimmune responses typically emerge weeks to months following a viral trigger. The narrow time window underscores an acute, highly synchronous pathophysiological process.

Patients with OPE often present with prominent clinical manifestations such as headache, seizures, psychosis, and memory disorders, accompanied by aseptic or viral CSF features and bilateral temporal lobe imaging abnormalities. Recognizing this entity is critical because timely diagnosis requires a combination of antiviral therapy and early immunomodulatory interventions to significantly improve clinical outcomes.
teaching_points: Overlapping Peak Encephalitis (OPE) is characterized by the concurrent detection of viral pathogens (via mNGS) and neuronal autoantibodies within 72 hours of symptom onset.
OPE differs pathophysiologically from classic biphasic encephalitis, which develops weeks to months after the primary viral infection.
Simultaneous testing for both viral pathogens and neuronal autoantibodies in acute encephalitis presentations is vital for timely diagnosis and combined antiviral-immunomodulatory therapy.
clinical_pitfalls: Assuming that antibody-mediated encephalitis only occurs weeks after viral clearance, thereby missing acute concomitant autoimmune triggers.
Failing to perform metagenomic next-generation sequencing alongside autoantibody panels in patients presenting with acute limbic encephalitis features.

title: Isolated Freezing of Gait with Parietal Cortical Atrophy and Preserved Dopamine Transporter Binding

presentation.chief_complaint: One-year history of freezing of gait and recurrent unprovoked falls
presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a one-year history of progressive freezing of gait (FOG) and recurrent unprovoked falls, manifesting as hesitation when starting, turning, and navigating narrow spaces. He denied any prodromal non-motor symptoms such as REM sleep behavior disorder, hyposmia, or constipation, as well as visual disturbances. Despite multiple trials of carbidopa/levodopa, his FOG showed no noticeable clinical improvement.
presentation.past_medical_history: Appendectomy 30 years prior; otherwise non-contributory with no family history of neurodegenerative diseases.
presentation.neuro_exam: Marked FOG during gait initiation, turning, and reaching destination. Cranial nerves, motor strength, sensation, coordination, and reflexes were otherwise normal. No rigidity, resting tremor, or bradykinesia noted on initial presentation. Mini-Mental State Examination: 29/30, Montreal Cognitive Assessment: 30/30, Frontal Assessment Battery: 18/18.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Routine blood work, comprehensive metabolic panel, and vitamin B12 levels were entirely normal.

imaging.modality: Brain MRI (Axial FLAIR, Coronal T2) & 18F-FP-CIT PET
imaging.caption: The patient’s neuroimaging findings ( A) Brain MRI acquired in December 2016 shows marked bilateral parietal lobe atrophy, shown on axial FLAIR images (upper panels) and coronal T2-weighted images (lower panels). B The volume and contour of the midbrain are normal ( C ) 18 F-FP-CIT PET scans obtained in December 2016 reveal normal dopamine transporter binding ( D ) A single-case voxel-based morphometry study, in comparison with 10 age- and sex-matched controls, shows decreased volume in the right superior parietal lobe and left superior occipital gyrus in the patient’s brain. Abbreviations: MR
imaging.findings_summary: Demonstrated marked bilateral parietal lobe atrophy with normal midbrain volume and normal presynaptic dopamine transporter binding.

challenge.question: Given the clinical presentation of isolated, levodopa-unresponsive freezing of gait lasting over a year, normal striatal dopamine transporter (DAT) uptake, preserved cognition, and marked bilateral parietal atrophy without brainstem changes, what is the most appropriate clinico-pathological syndrome?

options.text: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease with early axial involvement
options.rationale: Incorrect. Idiopathic Parkinson's disease typically presents with abnormal presynaptic DAT uptake on functional imaging and responds well to dopaminergic therapy, unlike this patient.
Incorrect. Progressive supranuclear palsy characteristically demonstrates midbrain atrophy ('hummingbird sign') and early vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, which were absent here.

options.text: Primary progressive freezing of gait (PPFG) disorder
options.rationale: Correct! Primary progressive freezing of gait (PPFG) is a rare clinical syndrome characterized by isolated FOG persisting for at least three years without other cardinal features of parkinsonism, often linked to atypical tauopathies or cortical network degeneration rather than nigrostriatal dopamine depletion.

Incorrect. Normal pressure hydrocephalus classically presents with the triad of gait ataxia (magnetic gait), urinary incontinence, and cognitive impairment, alongside ventriculomegaly on neuroimaging.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Primary progressive freezing of gait (PPFG) disorder
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Primary progressive freezing of gait (PPFG) is an uncommon clinical entity defined by isolated freezing of gait persisting for at least three years without accompanying parkinsonism, cerebellar signs, or early dementia. The pathophysiology of FOG remains elusive, frequently confounding clinicians because it can manifest across various neurodegenerative spectra including progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal degeneration (CBD), and primary lateral sclerosis (PLS). 

In this case, the combination of isolated FOG, normal DAT imaging, and marked bilateral parietal cortical atrophy—with voxel-based morphometry highlighting superior parietal and occipital volume loss—points toward higher-level gait disorders involving dysfunction of the frontoparietal networks responsible for motor planning, visuospatial integration, and gait initiation. The lack of response to levodopa and preserved dopamine transporter binding further emphasize that non-dopaminergic pathways and cortical networks subserve this distinct neurodegenerative phenotype.
teaching_points: Primary progressive freezing of gait (PPFG) is a rare syndrome defined by isolated FOG lasting at least three years without parkinsonism.
Parietal cortical atrophy and normal presynaptic dopamine transporter (DAT) imaging support non-dopaminergic frontoparietal network dysfunction in select FOG phenotypes.
PPFG may represent a localized clinical variant of atypical parkinsonian syndromes such as PSP or CBD before broader clinical features emerge.
clinical_pitfalls: Assuming all disabling gait freezing in older adults is due to idiopathic Parkinson's disease or normal pressure hydrocephalus.
Failing to recognize that isolated FOG can exhibit a poor response to dopaminergic medications due to underlying cortical-subcortical network degeneration rather than nigrostriatal failure.

title: Acute Basilar Artery Occlusion and Brainstem Infarction in a Young Adult

presentation.chief_complaint: Acute dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and left-sided numbness and weakness
presentation.history_of_present_illness: The patient with a 20-pack-year smoking history developed sudden-onset dizziness, nausea, vomiting, dysarthria, and left-sided numbness and weakness. He was brought to the emergency department within the acute therapeutic window with an initial National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score of 7, demonstrating horizontal nystagmus, left tongue deviation, and limb ataxia.
presentation.past_medical_history: 20-pack-year smoking history; no prior history of stroke, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or structural heart disease.
presentation.neuro_exam: NIHSS 7 (I2=1, I4=1, I5a=1, I6a=1, I7=1, I8=1, I10=1). Awake and alert, horizontal nystagmus on gaze, left tongue deviation, left-sided facial and limb sensory loss, left-sided limb ataxia, and left-sided motor weakness (MRC grade 4/5).
presentation.key_labs_csf: Comprehensive thrombophilia screen, vasculitis autoantibodies, serum homocysteine, lipid profile, and HbA1c were entirely normal or negative.

imaging.caption: Relevant information for patient 1. Craniocerebral CTA indicating basilar artery occlusion ( A ). Cerebral perfusion imaging suggesting the presence of an ischemic penumbra ( B ). Preoperative Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) showing basilar artery occlusion ( C ), postoperative imaging confirming recanalization with an mTICI grade 3 ( D ). Cranial Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI) on postoperative day 1 showing acute cerebral infarction in the brainstem and cerebellum ( E ). Histopathology of the retrieved embolus shows coagulated blood and fibrinous material without atypical cells, confi
imaging.findings_summary: CTA reveals acute basilar artery occlusion with perfusion imaging demonstrating a significant salvageable ischemic penumbra in the brainstem and cerebellum.

imaging.caption: Partial information for patient 2. Intraoperative DSA confirming a left internal carotid artery occlusion and right middle cerebral artery stenosis ( A , C ). Lower-limb DSA indicating an embolism in the left femoral artery ( E ). Postoperative DSA showing restored patency of the left internal carotid and right middle cerebral arteries with an mTICI grade 3 ( B , D ). Partial removal of the emboli in the lower limb arteries ( F )
imaging.findings_summary: DWI confirms acute ischemic infarctions in the brainstem and cerebellum, while cardiac CT enhancement demonstrates a large left atrial mass measuring 73 x 36 mm.

challenge.question: What is the most definitive underlying pathophysiological mechanism for the acute ischemic stroke in this young patient?

options.text: Cardioembolic occlusion secondary to paradoxical patent foramen ovale (PFO)
options.rationale: Incorrect. The patient is young with no vascular risk factors other than smoking, and advanced imaging/histopathology confirmed an embolic rather than atherosclerotic etiology.

options.text: Spontaneous basilar or vertebral artery dissection with secondary in-situ thrombosis
options.rationale: Correct! The patient suffered an acute basilar artery occlusion due to secondary thrombosis from a large left atrial myxoma. Acute endovascular thrombectomy successfully restored vessel patency, followed by curative surgical resection of the cardiac tumor to prevent recurrent cardioembolic events.

Incorrect. Vasculitis autoantibody screening and workup were entirely negative, and tissue pathology retrieved from mechanical thrombectomy confirmed a bland thrombotic embolus rather than vessel wall inflammation.

options.text: Hypercoagulable state due to primary antiphospholipid antibody syndrome
options.rationale: Incorrect. Echocardiography and cardiac imaging definitively identified a large left atrial myxoma as the source of embolization, making PFO an incorrect and insufficient explanation.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Acute basilar artery occlusion secondary to left atrial myxoma
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Atrial myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor and a well-recognized, albeit rare, source of cardioembolic stroke in young adults. Embolization can occur via two distinct mechanisms: direct shedding of tumor tissue fragments or, more commonly, secondary thrombosis forming on the surface of the friable myxoma. In this case, the patient presented with an isolated basilar artery occlusion caused by a secondary thrombotic embolus, verified by the lack of atypical cells on histopathological analysis of the retrieved clot.

Management of atrial myxoma-related stroke requires a dual approach: acute revascularization (such as mechanical thrombectomy or thrombolysis when appropriate) to salvage ischemic brain tissue, followed by prompt surgical excision of the cardiac mass to mitigate the high risk of recurrent, potentially fatal embolic events. Integrated multimodality imaging, including brain CT/MRI, vascular CTA/DSA, and cardiac echocardiography or CT, is critical for accurate etiological diagnosis and successful multidisciplinary management.
teaching_points: Atrial myxomas can cause acute ischemic stroke through either direct tumor embolization or secondary surface thrombosis.
Young patients presenting with stroke of undetermined etiology require thorough cardiac imaging, as cardiac tumors frequently mimic primary cerebrovascular disease.
Prompt mechanical thrombectomy is effective for large vessel occlusions due to myxoma-related emboli, followed by urgent surgical resection of the tumor.
clinical_pitfalls: Failing to perform cardiac imaging in young stroke patients can miss treatable structural cardiac lesions such as myxomas.
Delaying surgical removal of an atrial myxoma after an embolic stroke significantly increases the risk of recurrent systemic or cerebral embolism.

title: Acute Somnolence, Vertical Gaze Palsy, and Severe Memory Impairment Following Left Vertebral Artery V4 Stent Deployment

presentation.chief_complaint: Acute postoperative altered consciousness, vertical gaze palsy, and severe anterograde/retrograde memory impairment immediately following endovascular stenting of the left V4 vertebral artery
presentation.history_of_present_illness: A 51-year-old man presented with paroxysmal dizziness for over one month. Pre-admission MRI showed scattered infarctions in the left cerebellar hemisphere, and Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) revealed severe stenosis with dissection of the V4 segment of the left vertebral artery, extracranial termination of the right vertebral artery, and a right fetal-type posterior cerebral artery. After 7 days of dual antiplatelet therapy (indobufen and clopidogrel), he underwent balloon angioplasty and stent deployment in the left V4 vertebral artery under general anesthesia. Immediately after emergence from anesthesia and on postoperative day 1, he developed profound somnolence, apathy, and severe memory impairment without hemiplegia.
presentation.past_medical_history: Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease, prior ischemic stroke, and aspirin-associated gastrointestinal bleeding.
presentation.neuro_exam: Somnolent but arousable to verbal stimuli; marked anterograde and retrograde amnesia, apathy, and vertical gaze paresis (impaired upgaze and downgaze). Motor strength was 5/5 in all four extremities with no Babinski sign.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Postprocedural angiography confirmed patent left vertebral artery stent and patent basilar trunk; non-contrast head CT immediately post-procedure showed no intracranial hemorrhage.

imaging.caption: DSA during vertebral artery stenting. (A, B) Anteroposterior and lateral views of the posterior circulation showing stenosis with dissection of the V4 segment of the left vertebral artery (yellow arrows). (C) Balloon angioplasty. (D) Stent deployment (yellow arrows indicate the marker bands at both ends of the stent). (E, F) Postprocedural anteroposterior and lateral views of the posterior circulation.
imaging.findings_summary: Successful left V4 vertebral artery stent deployment restoring lumen caliber; however, distal microembolization into a single P1 perforator trunk occurred despite patent basilar flow.

imaging.modality: Brain MRI — Postoperative Day 1 Axial Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI)
imaging.caption: Brain MRI on postoperative day 1. (A, B) MRI-DWI showing acute infarction in the bilateral paramedian thalamic regions (yellow arrows). (C) MRI-DWI showing the midbrain 'V' sign of the AOP infarction (yellow arrows).
imaging.findings_summary: Symmetric bilateral paramedian thalamic diffusion restriction accompanied by the pathognomonic hyperintense 'V' sign along the pial surface of the interpeduncular fossa in the rostral midbrain.

challenge.question: Based on the classic clinical triad (altered consciousness, vertical gaze palsy, and Korsakoff-like memory impairment) and the postoperative Day 1 MRI-DWI findings (Figure 2), occlusion of which anatomical vascular variant accounts for this syndrome?

options.text: Artery of Percheron (Type IIb paramedian thalamic-mesencephalic perforator variant arising from a single P1 segment)
options.rationale: Correct! The Artery of Percheron (AOP, Type IIb variant) is a solitary arterial trunk arising from the proximal P1 segment of one posterior cerebral artery that supplies the paramedian thalami bilaterally and the rostral midbrain. Distal microembolization during posterior circulation intervention produces the classic triad of fluctuating consciousness/somnolence, vertical gaze palsy, and severe memory impairment, along with the pathognomonic midbrain 'V' sign on axial DWI.

options.text: Deep cerebral venous thrombosis of the internal cerebral veins and Vein of Galen
options.rationale: Incorrect. While deep venous thrombosis causes bilateral thalamic edema, it typically involves the entire thalamus symmetrically with prominent vasogenic edema and hemorrhage on SWI, rather than sharply demarcated paramedian thalamic and interpeduncular 'V-sign' arterial territory infarction immediately following vertebral stenting.

options.text: Tuberothalamic (polar) artery occlusion arising from the posterior communicating artery
options.rationale: Incorrect. The tuberothalamic artery supplies the anterior thalamic nuclei and is almost always unilateral; it does not produce bilateral paramedian thalamic and rostral midbrain ('V' sign) infarction.

options.text: Thalamogeniculate artery occlusion arising from the P2 segment of the posterior cerebral artery
options.rationale: Incorrect. Thalamogeniculate perforators supply the ventrolateral thalamus, causing Dejerine-Roussy syndrome (contralateral hemisensory loss and thalamic pain) rather than bilateral paramedian coma and vertical gaze palsy.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Acute Bilateral Paramedian Thalamic and Rostral Midbrain Infarction Due to Artery of Percheron (AOP) Occlusion Following Vertebral Artery Stenting
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Percheron classified the neurovascular supply to the paramedian thalamus into four anatomical variants. Type IIb—the Artery of Percheron (AOP)—is a rare anatomical variant (present in 4%–12% of the population) in which a single common arterial trunk arises from the P1 segment of one posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and bifurcates to supply both paramedian thalamic territories as well as the rostral midbrain via the superior mesencephalic (rubral) arteries.

During neurointerventional procedures for vertebral artery stenosis complicated by dissection, plaque fragmentation or microthrombus dislodgement can embolize distally into the P1 perforators even when the main basilar trunk remains completely patent on completion angiography. Recognition of the classic triad—altered mental status/hypersomnolence, vertical gaze palsy (involvement of the rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, riMLF), and severe amnestic syndrome (dorsomedial and intralaminar thalamic nuclei)—together with the midbrain 'V' sign along the interpeduncular fossa on axial DWI (67% sensitivity in AOP stroke with midbrain involvement) enables rapid diagnosis.
teaching_points: The classic clinical triad of Artery of Percheron (AOP) infarction consists of altered consciousness (somnolence/coma), vertical gaze palsy, and severe memory impairment.

The 'midbrain V sign'—a V-shaped hyperintensity on axial FLAIR/DWI along the pial surface of the interpeduncular fossa—is a highly specific neuroimaging marker of AOP infarction with rostral midbrain involvement.

Conventional CTA, MRA, and even DSA usually fail to visualize the occludedAOP trunk directly due to its small caliber; diagnosis relies on the characteristic bilateral paramedian thalamic DWI pattern.
clinical_pitfalls: Misattributing postoperative somnolence after general anesthesia to delayed anesthetic clearance or metabolic encephalopathy when focal motor deficits are absent.
Assuming a normal completion angiogram of the basilar trunk and PCAs excludes perforator occlusion after posterior circulation angioplasty/stenting.

title: Acute Urinary Retention, Right Leg Thermal Hypesthesia, and Rapidly Progressive Encephalomyelitis with Coma in a 38-Year-Old Lactating Woman

presentation.chief_complaint: Acute urinary retention and right lower-extremity thermal hypesthesia rapidly progressing to encephalopathy, status epilepticus, and coma 14 days after viral gastroenteritis
presentation.history_of_present_illness: A 38-year-old woman who was partially breastfeeding presented to the emergency department with acute urinary retention requiring bladder catheterization. Two weeks before symptom onset, she experienced arthralgia, fatigue, and moderate enterovirus gastroenteritis. Within 5 days of admission, despite empiric intravenous ceftriaxone, ampicillin, and acyclovir, her neurological status rapidly deteriorated to severe encephalopathy, status epilepticus, and coma requiring intensive care unit intubation.
presentation.past_medical_history: Postpartum lactating mother; recent enterovirus gastroenteritis 14 days prior; no history of multiple sclerosis.
presentation.neuro_exam: On admission: right leg thermal hypesthesia and neurogenic urinary retention. By hospital day 5: comatose, generalized status epilepticus, hyperreflexia, and bilateral extensor plantar responses.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Lumbar puncture revealed marked CSF pleocytosis (968 leukocytes/μL, 92% lymphocytes, 8% neutrophils) with elevated CSF protein and transient CSF-specific oligoclonal bands. Broad infectious PCR/NGS panel in CSF was negative. Serum AQP4-IgG was negative.

imaging.modality: Brain Coronal FLAIR & Spinal Cord Sagittal/Axial T2-Weighted MRI
imaging.caption: MRI of the brain (A) and spinal cord (B) at day 2, day 5, and day 48. (A) T2-FLAIR hyperintense right thalamic lesion with poorly demarcated ('fluffy') margins and (B) T2 hyperintense right middle cerebellar peduncle lesion; on day 5 (C, D) progression of the thalamic lesion and new bilateral white matter lesions; spinal MRI shows longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM) predominantly involving central thoracic gray matter ('H-sign') and the conus medullaris; (E, F) near-complete radiologic resolution on day 48 after immunotherapy.
imaging.findings_summary: Poorly demarcated 'fluffy' deep gray matter (thalamic) and middle cerebellar peduncle T2-FLAIR lesions, right optic nerve hyperintensity, and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM) featuring the axial central gray matter 'H-sign' and conus medullaris involvement.

challenge.question: Given the acute flaccid paraparesis, conus medullaris dysfunction, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis with an axial H-sign, and marked CSF pleocytosis, which of the following is the most likely underlying etiology?

options.text: Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS) — Confirmed by McDonald Dissemination in Time and Space criteria
options.rationale: Incorrect. Multiple sclerosis produces short-segment (<2 vertebral segments), peripheral dorsolateral spinal cord lesions, ovoid periventricular Dawson fingers, and CSF pleocytosis rarely exceeding 50 cells/μL.

options.text: MOG Antibody-Associated Disease (MOGAD) — Confirmed by serum live cell-based assay (CBA) for full-length conformational MOG-IgG
options.rationale: Correct! Post-infectious onset, conus medullaris involvement causing early acute urinary retention, LETM restricted to central spinal gray matter (the 'H-sign' on axial T2), fluffy thalamic/middle cerebellar peduncle lesions, prominent CSF pleocytosis (which can exceed 500 cells/μL, mimicking infectious meningitis), and dramatic steroid/PLEX responsiveness with near-complete MRI resolution are classic hallmarks of MOGAD. Live cell-based assay (CBA) has superior sensitivity over fixed CBA.

options.text: Seropositive Aquaporin-4 (AQP4-IgG) Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD)
options.rationale: Incorrect. While AQP4-IgG NMOSD causes LETM, it preferentially affects the area postrema and central cord with T1 hypointensity ('bright spotty lesions'), rarely exhibits the isolated gray-matter 'H-sign' with complete radiologic resolution, and serum AQP4-IgG was negative.

options.text: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC virus reactivation
options.rationale: Incorrect. PML occurs in severely immunocompromised hosts, presents with subacute asymmetric subcortical U-fiber demyelination without acute conus myelitis or marked CSF pleocytosis, and does not resolve after corticosteroids and plasma exchange.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Fulminant Post-Enterovirus Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein Antibody-Associated Disease (MOGAD) Presenting with Encephalomyelitis, Optic Neuritis, and Conus LETM
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) is a distinct autoimmune astrocytopathy-sparing demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system. Unlike multiple sclerosis or AQP4-IgG NMOSD, MOGAD frequently follows a viral prodrome (such as enterovirus gastroenteritis) and can present as an explosive polyfocal ADEM-like encephalomyelitis with status epilepticus, optic neuritis, and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM).

Key neuroradiological signatures that distinguish MOGAD from MS and AQP4+ NMOSD include: (1) predilection for the conus medullaris (explaining early severe neurogenic bladder retention), (2) T2 hyperintensity confined to the central spinal cord gray matter forming an axial 'H-sign' without contrast enhancement, (3) poorly demarcated ('fluffy') lesions in the thalamus and middle cerebellar peduncles, and (4) complete or near-complete resolution of MRI T2 lesions following high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone and plasma exchange (PLEX). Importantly, live cell-based assays (CBA) detect conformational MOG-IgG titers that may be missed or underestimated by fixed assays.
teaching_points: Spinal cord involvement in MOGAD classically features longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM) affecting the conus medullaris and central gray matter ('H-sign' on axial T2 MRI).
Marked CSF pleocytosis (>100 to >500 cells/μL) can occur in acute MOGAD attacks, closely mimicking acute bacterial or viral meningoencephalomyelitis.
Live cell-based assay (CBA) for serum MOG-IgG is the gold standard diagnostic test and should be ordered when fixed CBA is equivocal in high-suspicion phenotypes.
clinical_pitfalls: Dismissing autoimmune demyelination because CSF leukocyte counts exceed 500 cells/μL and withholding high-dose corticosteroids/plasma exchange once infectious PCRs return negative.
Relying solely on fixed cell-based assays when clinical and MRI features (conus LETM + H-sign + fluffy thalamic lesions) strongly point to MOGAD.

title: Focal Motor Seizures, Subacute Cognitive Decline, Asymmetric Lobar Vasogenic Edema, and Cortical Superficial Siderosis in a 71-Year-Old Patient

presentation.chief_complaint: New-onset right-sided focal seizures, subacute executive dysfunction, and persistent holocranial headache over 3 weeks
presentation.history_of_present_illness: A 71-year-old woman was admitted after experiencing recurrent focal aware and impaired-awareness motor seizures affecting the right arm and face, preceded by a 3-week history of progressive confusion, word-finding difficulty, and subacute headache. There was no history of fever, recent infection, systemic malignancy, or anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody infusion.
presentation.past_medical_history: Mild hypertension; no known history of atrial fibrillation or systemic autoimmune disease.
presentation.neuro_exam: Alert but mildly disoriented to time; expressive dysphasia, executive dysfunction (MoCA 19/30), and mild right pronator drift. No meningismus.
presentation.key_labs_csf: CSF analysis showed mildly elevated protein (68 mg/dL), 12 lymphocytes/μL, normal glucose, negative viral/bacterial PCR panel, and elevated CSF anti-amyloid-β autoantibodies.

imaging.modality: 3-Tesla Brain MRI — Axial FLAIR & Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging (SWI)
imaging.caption: Brain 3-T MRI of a patient presenting with focal seizures. At baseline, FLAIR imaging shows an extensive hyperintense lesion involving the left frontal lobe (A, red arrowhead), and SWI demonstrates cortical superficial siderosis (cSS) in the frontotemporal lobes (B, yellow arrowhead). Follow-up MRI after early steroid therapy shows regression of the left frontal inflammatory lesion on FLAIR (C) and progression of cSS on SWI (D).
imaging.findings_summary: Asymmetric confluent left frontal white matter FLAIR hyperintensity (vasogenic edema mimicking a tumor) colocalized with strictly lobar microbleeds and frontotemporal cortical superficial siderosis (cSS) on SWI.

challenge.question: In an older adult presenting with subacute cognitive decline, focal motor seizures, asymmetric confluent FLAIR vasogenic edema, and cortical superficial siderosis on SWI, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Acute ischemic left middle cerebral artery stroke — Administer dual antiplatelet therapy and high-intensity statin
options.rationale: Incorrect. The FLAIR lesion represents subcortical vasogenic edema without cytotoxic diffusion restriction, and antithrombotic therapy increases the risk of lobar intracerebral hemorrhage in patients with CAA and cortical superficial siderosis.

options.text: High-grade infiltrative left frontal glioblastoma — Proceed directly to stereotactic craniotomy and surgical resection
options.rationale: Incorrect. Confluent asymmetric vasogenic edema in CAA-ri frequently mimics a high-grade glioma on FLAIR alone, which is why blood-sensitive SWI sequences are mandatory to identify underlying cortical superficial siderosis and lobar microbleeds and avoid unnecessary brain surgery.

options.text: Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy-Related Inflammation (CAA-ri) — Initiate early high-dose intravenous corticosteroids without invasive brain biopsy
options.rationale: Correct! Probable CAA-ri can be diagnosed non-invasively using the Auriel criteria in patients ≥40 years old presenting with subacute cognitive decline, seizures, or headache when MRI demonstrates asymmetric confluent T2/FLAIR hyperintensity (vasogenic edema) alongside hemorrhagic CAA markers (strictly lobar microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis on SWI/T2*). Early high-dose corticosteroid initiation (within 6 weeks) leads to rapid clinical recovery and resolution of FLAIR edema (Figure 1C).

options.text: Herpes Simplex Virus-1 (HSV-1) Encephalitis — Maintain 21-day intravenous acyclovir monotherapy
options.rationale: Incorrect. HSV-1 encephalitis presents with acute febrile encephalopathy, hemorrhagic necrosis of the medial temporal/insular cortex, and positive CSF HSV-1 PCR.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy-Related Inflammation (CAA-ri) Responsive to Early High-Dose Corticosteroid Therapy
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related inflammation (CAA-ri) is a spontaneous autoimmune encephalopathy triggered by an inflammatory reaction against vascular amyloid-β (Aβ) deposits in the leptomeningeal and cortical arterioles. Notably, its clinicoradiologic appearance is virtually identical to Amyloid-Related Imaging Abnormalities with Edema (ARIA-E) observed in patients treated with anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies.

Validated diagnostic criteria (Auriel et al., Neurology) allow a diagnosis of probable CAA-ri without brain biopsy when an individual ≥40 years old presents with ≥1 clinical feature (headache, cognitive decline, focal deficits, or seizures), asymmetric confluent T2/FLAIR white matter hyperintensity extending to the subcortical U-fibers, and ≥1 hemorrhagic CAA marker on SWI/GRE (strictly lobar cerebral microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis). As demonstrated in the 2026 multicenter cohort study in Neurology: Neuroimmunology & Neuroinflammation, early corticosteroid initiation within 6 weeks of symptom onset is strongly associated with superior functional outcomes (OR 0.14 for worse mRS) and rapid resolution of FLAIR vasogenic edema.
teaching_points: Always review SWI/GRE blood-sensitive sequences when an elderly patient presents with an asymmetric tumor-like FLAIR white matter lesion; lobar microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis (cSS) establish probable CAA-ri.
CAA-ri is the spontaneous clinicoradiological counterpart of ARIA-E and responds dramatically to early high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone.
Fulfilling probable CAA-ri diagnostic criteria obviates the need for invasive stereotactic brain biopsy unless the patient fails to improve with corticosteroid therapy.
clinical_pitfalls: Ordering only conventional T1/T2/FLAIR MRI without SWI/T2* sequences, resulting in misdiagnosis of CAA-ri as a primary brain tumor and subjecting the patient to neurosurgical biopsy.
Delaying corticosteroid therapy beyond 6 weeks from symptom onset, which significantly worsens functional recovery and prolongs vasogenic edema.

title: Rapidly Progressive Consciousness Impairment, Seizures, and Bilateral Venous Infarction Refractory to Systemic Heparin in a 20-Year-Old Male with Nephrotic Relapse

presentation.chief_complaint: Severe progressive headache, generalized seizures, right hemiparesis, and rapid decline in consciousness despite therapeutic anticoagulation during a relapse of minimal change nephrotic syndrome
presentation.history_of_present_illness: A 20-year-old man with biopsy-proven minimal change disease (MCD) presented with recurrent lower-extremity edema, massive proteinuria, and severe hypoalbuminemia after tapering oral prednisone. During hospitalization, he developed acute severe diffuse headache followed by generalized tonic-clonic seizures, progressive limb weakness, and somnolence. Despite immediate initiation of therapeutic systemic anticoagulation, his mental status deteriorated rapidly to stupor with worsening bilateral venous congestion.
presentation.past_medical_history: Minimal change nephrotic syndrome diagnosed 6 years prior with steroid-dependent relapses; no prior history of venous thromboembolism.
presentation.neuro_exam: Stuporous (GCS 9), papilledema on fundoscopy, left-greater-than-right hemiparesis (MRC 2/5), and bilateral Babinski signs.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Serum albumin: 16.2 g/L; 24-hour urine protein: >8.5 g/day; D-dimer markedly elevated (>5,000 ng/mL); urinary loss of antithrombin III with severe hyperfibrinogenemia.

imaging.modality: Brain MR Venography (MRV), Axial DWI & Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging (SWI)
imaging.caption: (A, B) MRV showed no clear visualization of bilateral transverse and sigmoid sinuses. (C) DWI showed abnormal signals in the right parietal lobe and left frontal lobe, suggestive of acute/subacute venous infarction. (D) SWI showed multiple tortuous engorged cortical draining veins.
imaging.findings_summary: Complete absence of flow signal in the superior sagittal, bilateral transverse, and sigmoid sinuses on MRV, with non-arterial bihemispheric venous infarctions on DWI and prominent engorged cortical veins on SWI.

imaging.modality: Digital Subtraction Cerebral Angiography (DSA) — Venous Phase
imaging.caption: (A) Cerebral angiography revealed occlusion of the bilateral transverse sinuses. (B) Cerebral angiography revealed occlusion of the superior sagittal sinus.
imaging.findings_summary: Extensive pan-sinus thrombosis involving the superior sagittal sinus and bilateral transverse/sigmoid sinuses with severe venous outflow obstruction.

challenge.question: What is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism predisposing this patient to extensive cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST)?

options.text: Routine elective endovascular thrombectomy is indicated as first-line therapy over heparin for all stable patients with mild headache from CVST
options.rationale: Incorrect. The TO-ACT trial showed that routine endovascular therapy does not improve outcomes over standard anticoagulation in unselected CVST; endovascular rescue is reserved for patients with rapid neurological deterioration refractory to medical anticoagulation.

options.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation — Immediately discontinue all anticoagulation due to bihemispheric venous infarctions on DWI
options.rationale: Incorrect. Venous infarction (and even hemorrhagic venous infarction) in CVST is caused by venous outflow hypertension; discontinuing anticoagulation leads to fatal thrombus propagation.

options.text: Primary CNS vasculitis — Administer oral aspirin monotherapy and defer venography
options.rationale: Incorrect. MRV and DSA clearly demonstrate occlusion of the superior sagittal and bilateral transverse dural sinuses rather than arterial vasculitis.

options.text: Acquired urinary loss of Antithrombin III & hepatic hyperfibrinogenemia — Escalate to rescue endovascular catheter-directed thrombolysis / mechanical thrombectomy while continuing anticoagulation
options.rationale: Correct! Nephrotic syndrome creates a potent prothrombotic state driven by urinary loss of low-molecular-weight natural anticoagulants (especially Antithrombin III and free Protein S) coupled with compensatory hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen and Factors V/VIII. While systemic anticoagulation (LMWH/UFH) is first-line for CVST, rescue endovascular therapy (catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy) is life-saving in patients with extensive multi-sinus thrombosis who deteriorate into coma/stupor despite medical therapy.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Extensive Pan-Sinus Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST) Secondary to Relapsed Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome Managed with Rescue Endovascular Thrombolysis
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Patients with relapsed nephrotic syndrome (such as minimal change disease or membranous nephropathy) exhibit a severe acquired hypercoagulable state. Massive glomerular proteinuria leads to selective urinary depletion of low-molecular-weight anticoagulant proteins—most notably Antithrombin III (AT-III)—while the liver increases synthesis of high-molecular-weight procoagulant factors (fibrinogen, Factor V, Factor VIII). Notably, severe AT-III deficiency can also blunt the efficacy of unfractionated heparin, which depends on AT-III as a cofactor.

When extensive thrombosis involves both the superior sagittal sinus and bilateral transverse sinuses, cortical venous drainage fails, leading to bihemispheric venous infarctions, tortuous engorged veins on SWI, and rapid herniation risk. In patients who experience progressive coma or neurological deterioration despite systemic anticoagulation, rescue endovascular catheter-directed thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy rapidly restores dural sinus patency and can achieve complete neurological recovery.
teaching_points: Nephrotic syndrome predisposes to CVST via urinary loss of Antithrombin III and increased hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen; severe AT-III depletion can cause heparin resistance.

Bihemispheric cortical/subcortical infarctions that do not respect arterial territories (e.g., right parietal + left frontal on DWI) with engorged veins on SWI are classic imaging clues to superior sagittal sinus thrombosis.
Rescue endovascular thrombolysis/thrombectomy is indicated when extensive CVST progresses clinically to stupor/coma despite therapeutic anticoagulation.
clinical_pitfalls: Using unfractionated heparin without checking or repletive monitoring for Antithrombin III deficiency in severely nephrotic patients.
Waiting for irreversible transtentorial herniation before consulting neurointerventional surgery in pan-sinus CVST refractory to systemic anticoagulation.

title: Refractory Severe Hyponatremia (109 mmol/L), Drowsiness, and Brief Involuntary Left Faciobrachial Spasms Without Ictal EEG Correlate in a 77-Year-Old Man

presentation.chief_complaint: Two-month history of refractory severe hyponatremia (serum Na+ nadir 109 mmol/L), progressive drowsiness, and frequent brief involuntary spasms of the left arm and face
presentation.history_of_present_illness: A 77-year-old man was admitted for recurrent profound hyponatremia (serum sodium 108.8–109 mmol/L) accompanied by poor appetite, fatigue, and progressive somnolence over 2 months. Despite intravenous hypertonic and isotonic sodium replacement during a prior hospitalization, his hyponatremia rapidly relapsed. One week prior to current admission, he developed repetitive, stereotypic, brief (<3 seconds) involuntary contractions of the left upper limb and ipsilateral grimacing occurring dozens of times per day.
presentation.past_medical_history: Hypertension (10 years), psoriasis (8 years), and newly diagnosed autoimmune gastritis with vitamin B12 deficiency.
presentation.neuro_exam: Drowsy with impaired short-term memory recall; frequent brief dystonic posturing of the left arm and ipsilateral facial grimacing lasting 1–3 seconds without loss of awareness between episodes.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Serum sodium: 109 mmol/L (refractory to sodium supplementation); macrocytic anemia (Hb 88 g/L, MCV 118 fL). CSF cell count and protein were mildly elevated; autoimmune encephalitis panel was strongly positive in CSF (1:64) and serum.

imaging.modality: Brain & Pituitary MRI — Axial T2-FLAIR & T2-Weighted Sequences
imaging.caption: (a) Axial T2WI FLAIR MRI of the brain showing patchy high signals in the bilateral hippocampus. (b) Axial T2WI MRI of the brain showing bilateral hippocampal swelling with increased signal intensity. (c) Sagittal MRI of the pituitary gland. (d) Coronal MRI of the pituitary gland showing small patchy areas of high T2 signal intensity (red arrow).
imaging.findings_summary: Bilateral mesial temporal / hippocampal swelling and T2-FLAIR hyperintensity typical of limbic encephalitis, accompanied by hypothalamic-pituitary axis involvement.

imaging.caption: Electroencephalogram (EEG) findings. Interictal period: showing mild background slowing with slightly increased fast-wave activity. Ictal period: recorded during a clinical episode of left limb spasm; no electrographic seizure discharge or epileptiform activity is observed.
imaging.findings_summary: Absence of scalp ictal epileptiform discharges during clinical left limb spasms, a classic electroclinical feature of subcortical/basal ganglia-mediated faciobrachial dystonic seizures (FBDS).

challenge.question: Which neuronal surface autoantibody is characteristically responsible for the presentation of faciobrachial dystonic seizures, hyponatremia, and medial temporal lobe T2-FLAIR hyperintensity?

options.rationale: Correct! Anti-LGI1 limbic encephalitis typically affects older men (median age ~65–75 years) and presents with pathognomonic Faciobrachial Dystonic Seizures (FBDS), severe refractory hyponatremia ( present in 60%–70% due to LGI1 expression in the hypothalamus/kidney causing SIADH or central adrenal insufficiency), and bilateral hippocampal T2-FLAIR hyperintensity. Scalp ictal EEG is negative in the majority of FBDS episodes, and FBDS are notoriously refractory to standard antiseizure medications alone but respond rapidly to corticosteroid immunotherapy.

Incorrect. Anti-NMDAR encephalitis predominantly affects young women and children with prominent psychiatric symptoms, dyskinesias, and extreme delta brush on EEG rather than FBDS and refractory hyponatremia in a 77-year-old man.
Incorrect. Normal scalp ictal EEG during brief dystonic jerks is a classic pitfall that leads to misdiagnosing anti-LGI1 FBDS as psychogenic or functional movement disorders.

options.text: Anti-Gamma-aminobutyric acid type B receptor (GABABR) antibody
options.rationale: Incorrect. Anti-GABA-B encephalitis is strongly associated with small-cell lung cancer and generalized convulsive status epilepticus, and standard antiseizure medications without immunotherapy fail to control LGI1-mediated FBDS.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Anti-LGI1 Antibody-Associated Limbic Encephalitis Presenting with Faciobrachial Dystonic Seizures (FBDS) and Refractory Hyponatremia
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1 (LGI1) is a secreted neuronal protein that complexes with ADAM22 and ADAM23 to regulate AMPA receptor synaptic transmission and Kv1.1 voltage-gated potassium channels in the hippocampus, basal ganglia, and hypothalamus. Anti-LGI1 encephalitis is the second most common autoimmune encephalitis and predominantly affects older adults in their 6th to 8th decades.

Two hallmark clinical clues often precede full-blown limbic amnesia by weeks to months: (1) profound, treatment-refractory hyponatremia (seen in 60%–70% of patients due to hypothalamic osmoreceptor/ADH dysregulation), and (2) Faciobrachial Dystonic Seizures (FBDS)—ultra-brief (<3 seconds), frequent (up to 50–100 times daily) unilateral contractions of the arm and ipsilateral face. Because FBDS originate in deep basal ganglia-thalamocortical networks, routine scalp ictal EEG (Figure 2) shows no epileptiform discharges in >75% of events. Early recognition and prompt initiation of high-dose corticosteroid immunotherapy rapidly abolish FBDS, normalize serum sodium, and prevent irreversible hippocampal atrophy and cognitive dementia.
teaching_points: Faciobrachial Dystonic Seizures (FBDS) combined with refractory hyponatremia in an older adult are pathognomonic for anti-LGI1 autoimmune encephalitis.
A normal scalp ictal EEG during brief unilateral arm/face spasms does NOT exclude FBDS, as the generator involves deep striatal-motor networks.
FBDS are usually refractory to antiseizure medications (and carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine carry a high risk of severe cutaneous reactions in LGI1 patients) but respond dramatically to corticosteroids.
clinical_pitfalls: Misdiagnosing scalp-EEG-negative faciobrachial dystonic seizures as psychogenic nonepileptic seizures, tics, or benign myoclonus.
Treating chronic hyponatremia symptomatically with fluid restriction and salt tablets without investigating for underlying limbic encephalitis when cognitive drowsiness or brief limb jerks emerge.

title: Recurrent Brief Positional Vertigo Triggered by Turning in Bed Mimicking Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo in a 63-Year-Old Hypertensive Man

presentation.chief_complaint: Recurrent brief attacks of positional vertigo triggered by lying down, sitting up, or turning over in bed with a normal initial head CT
presentation.history_of_present_illness: A 63-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presented with recurrent, discrete episodes of brief spinning vertigo lasting less than 1–2 minutes, reliably provoked by changing head position (lying down, getting up, or rolling over in bed). At initial emergency evaluation, limb strength, sensory examination, and non-contrast cranial CT were completely unremarkable, and Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) was suspected. However, Dix-Hallpike and supine roll maneuvers failed to elicit typical fatigable canalithiasis nystagmus, and he subsequently developed spontaneous direction-changing horizontal nystagmus and subtle left limb dysmetria.
presentation.past_medical_history: Poorly controlled essential hypertension; no prior history of Meniere disease or vestibular neuritis.
presentation.neuro_exam: Initial exam showed isolated positional dizziness; repeat serial examination revealed spontaneous central horizontal nystagmus, mild left finger-to-nose dysmetria, and truncal unsteadiness without dysarthria, Horner syndrome, or crossed sensory loss.
presentation.key_labs_csf: Non-contrast head CT was normal (no hemorrhage or visible posterior fossa hypodensity). ECG showed normal sinus rhythm.

imaging.caption: Diffusion-weighted imaging showing hyperintense infarct lesions in the medial left cerebellar hemisphere and cerebellar vermis.
imaging.findings_summary: Acute hyperintense infarction on DWI restricted to the medial left cerebellar hemisphere and inferior cerebellar vermis (nodulus/uvula) supplied by the medial branch of the PICA.

imaging.modality: Brain MRI — Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC) Map
imaging.caption: Apparent diffusion coefficient map showing corresponding hypointense lesions in the medial left cerebellar hemisphere and cerebellar vermis.
imaging.findings_summary: Corresponding dark ADC signal confirming acute cytotoxic edema in the vestibulocerebellum (mPICA territory), sparing the lateral medulla.

challenge.question: Which vascular territory or brainstem nucleus is selectively infarcted, producing isolated positional vertigo mimicking benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)?

options.text: Occlusion of the Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (AICA) causing isolated labyrinthine artery ischemia
options.rationale: Incorrect. AICA infarction involves the middle cerebellar peduncle, lateral pons, and internal auditory artery, classically causing ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss (deafness), facial palsy, and Horner syndrome.

options.text: Infarction of the medial branch of the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (mPICA) selectively damages the inferior vermis (nodulus/uvula) and vestibulocerebellar connections while sparing the lateral medulla
options.rationale: Correct! The PICA bifurcates into a medial branch (mPICA) and a lateral branch. The mPICA supplies the inferior cerebellar vermis (nodulus and uvula) and medial cerebellar hemisphere, which directly inhibit and modulate the brainstem vestibular nuclei during head pitch/roll movements. Infarction of the mPICA territory spares the dorsolateral medulla (hence no dysphagia, hoarseness, Horner syndrome, or crossed sensory loss) and presents as isolated central positional vertigo ('pseudo-BPPV') or isolated acute vestibular syndrome ('pseudo-vestibular neuritis').

options.text: A normal non-contrast head CT in the emergency department reliably excludes cerebellar infarction in patients with positional vertigo
options.rationale: Incorrect. Non-contrast head CT has <16%–25% sensitivity for acute posterior fossa ischemic stroke due to petrous bone beam-hardening artifact.

options.text: Superior Cerebellar Artery (SCA) occlusion selectively affecting the dentate nucleus
options.rationale: Incorrect. SCA infarction involves the superior cerebellar hemisphere and superior vermis, producing prominent ipsilateral limb ataxia and dysarthria rather than isolated inferior vermian (nodulus/uvula) positional vertigo.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Acute Medial Branch of the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (mPICA) Territory Cerebellar Infarction Presenting as Pseudo-BPPV
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Approximately 10.4% of isolated cerebellar infarctions present solely with vertigo and imbalance without obvious brainstem or long-tract signs, most frequently in the territory of the medial branch of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (mPICA). Because the mPICA supplies the inferior cerebellar vermis—specifically the nodulus and uvula, which integrate otolith and semicircular canal signals with the vestibular nuclei—ischemia in this territory disrupts central velocity-storage mechanisms and can produce brief positional vertigo triggered by turning over in bed (central positional vertigo / pseudo-BPPV).

Clinicians should suspect a central vascular cause (mPICA stroke) rather than benign peripheral BPPV when a patient with vascular risk factors has positional vertigo that fails to show classic fatigable upbeat-torsional nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike testing, fails to respond to Epley canalith repositioning maneuvers, or develops central ocular motor signs (direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, normal head impulse test, skew deviation, or subtle truncal/limb ataxia on serial exam).
teaching_points: Infarction in the medial branch of the PICA (mPICA) affects the inferior vermis (nodulus/uvula) and medial cerebellar hemisphere, frequently presenting as isolated vertigo ('pseudo-vestibular neuritis' or 'pseudo-BPPV') without lateral medullary signs.

In older patients with hypertension or vascular risk factors presenting with positional vertigo, absence of typical canal-specific nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike testing mandates serial neurological examinations and Brain MRI-DWI.
Non-contrast head CT is insensitive for acute cerebellar infarction; HINTS examination and MRI-DWI are the diagnostic standards.
clinical_pitfalls: Discharging a hypertensive patient with 'BPPV' based on positional symptom triggers and a normal head CT without verifying characteristic peripheral nystagmus on positional maneuvers.
Assuming all PICA strokes must exhibit Wallenberg syndrome (dysphagia, hoarseness, Horner syndrome, crossed sensory loss), which only occurs when the medullary perforators are involved.

title: Rapidly Progressive Cognitive Decline, Myoclonus, Generalized Periodic Triphasic Discharges with Anterior-Posterior Lag, and Cortical Ribboning

presentation.chief_complaint: Rapidly progressive dementia, visual disturbances, ataxia, and startle-sensitive myoclonic jerks evolving over 6 weeks
presentation.history_of_present_illness: A 64-year-old woman presented with a 6-week history of rapidly progressive cognitive decline, disorientation, cortical visual perceptual disturbances, and gait unsteadiness, followed by prominent stimulus-sensitive myoclonus and akinetic mutism. Because autoimmune encephalitis (such as anti-NMDAR encephalitis) is a potentially treatable mimic of rapidly progressive dementia, continuous video-EEG, lumbar puncture, and brain MRI were performed urgently prior to empiric immunotherapy.
presentation.past_medical_history: Unremarkable; no prior corneal transplant, dura mater graft, or family history of neurodegenerative disease.
presentation.neuro_exam: Severe global cognitive impairment evolving toward akinetic mutism, stimulus-induced myoclonus of the upper extremities, appendicular and truncal ataxia, and generalized hypertonia.
presentation.key_labs_csf: CSF analysis showed normal leukocyte count (2 cells/μL), normal glucose, negative serum and CSF anti-NMDAR and autoimmune encephalitis antibody panels, and positive CSF 14-3-3 protein and RT-QuIC assay. Continuous video-EEG demonstrated ~1 Hz Generalized Periodic Discharges (GPDs) with triphasic morphology and an anterior-to-posterior (A-P) phase lag.

imaging.caption: Axial DWI sequence showing non-asymmetric high signal in bilateral cortex (white arrows) of patients with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
imaging.findings_summary: Extensive gyriform hyperintensity ('cortical ribboning') along the bilateral cerebral cortex on DWI without mass effect or white matter edema.

imaging.caption: Axial T2 sequence showing extensive, non-asymmetric high signal in bilateral temporal lobe and occipital lobe (white arrows) of patients with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
imaging.findings_summary: Subtle corresponding cortical signal abnormality on T2-weighted imaging in the bilateral temporal and occipital cortices, markedly more conspicuous on DWI.

challenge.question: When evaluating a patient with rapidly progressive encephalopathy, which combination of neuroimaging (Figures 1 & 2), CSF, and continuous EEG findings most reliably distinguishes sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (sCJD) from anti-NMDAR encephalitis?

options.text: Confluent subcortical white matter vasogenic edema with ring-enhancing mass effect on gadolinium T1 MRI
options.rationale: Incorrect. Prion disease (sCJD) is strictly confined to gray matter (cerebral cortex and basal ganglia/thalamus) without vasogenic edema, mass effect, or contrast enhancement.

options.text: Extreme delta brush pattern on EEG, lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis, and isolated mesial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity
options.rationale: Incorrect. Extreme delta brush, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, and prominent clinical seizures are characteristic of anti-NMDAR encephalitis rather than sCJD.

options.text: Extensive cortical ribboning on DWI, acellular CSF with positive RT-QuIC/14-3-3, and ~1 Hz Generalized Periodic Discharges (GPDs) with triphasic morphology and anterior-posterior lag on EEG
options.rationale: Correct! As demonstrated in the comparative study (PMC13445854), sCJD is distinguished from anti-NMDAR encephalitis by extensive cortical gyriform diffusion restriction ('cortical ribboning', Figure 1) and/or striatal DWI hyperintensity, acellular CSF (whereas anti-NMDAR encephalitis shows significantly higher CSF leukocyte counts and frequent seizures), positive CSF RT-QuIC/14-3-3, and ~1 Hz GPDs with triphasic morphology and an anterior-to-posterior (A-P) lag on continuous EEG.

options.text: 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges on EEG and isolated mammillary body enhancement
options.rationale: Incorrect. 3-Hz spike-and-wave is seen in childhood absence epilepsy, and mammillary body enhancement is typical of Wernicke encephalopathy.

resolution.final_diagnosis: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (sCJD) Distinguished from Autoimmune Encephalitis by Cortical Ribboning and Triphasic GPDs
resolution.clinical_discussion:
Rapidly progressive dementia (RPD) evolving over weeks to months requires urgent differentiation between fatal prion disease (sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, sCJD) and reversible autoimmune encephalitis (such as anti-NMDAR or anti-LGI1 encephalitis). Both conditions can present with subacute cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms, movement disorders, and abnormal MRI/EEG findings.

Comparative analysis of continuous video-EEG, MRI, and CSF profiles demonstrates that sCJD is characterized by: (1) DWI 'cortical ribboning' (gyriform diffusion restriction in ≥2 cortical regions, especially temporal, parietal, and occipital cortices) and/or caudate/putamen hyperintensity, which is far more sensitive on DWI than on T2/FLAIR; (2) Generalized Periodic Discharges (GPDs) at 1–2 Hz with triphasic morphology and an anterior-to-posterior (A-P) time lag on EEG; and (3) normal CSF leukocyte counts with >95% specificity of Second-Generation Real-Time Quaking-Induced Conversion (RT-QuIC).
teaching_points: Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI) is the most sensitive MRI sequence for early sCJD, demonstrating gyriform 'cortical ribboning' and/or striatal hyperintensity long before T2 changes become obvious.
On continuous EEG, Generalized Periodic Discharges (GPDs) with triphasic morphology and an anterior-posterior (A-P) lag strongly favor sCJD over anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
Always exclude treatable autoimmune encephalitis (CSF pleocytosis, neural autoantibodies) in any patient evaluated for rapidly progressive dementia.
clinical_pitfalls: Misinterpreting DWI cortical ribboning as an acute arterial ischemic stroke or post-ictal cortical edema without checking whether the signal crosses vascular territories.
Relying solely on CSF 14-3-3 protein (which can be falsely positive in viral/autoimmune encephalitis or acute stroke) without correlating with DWI cortical ribboning and CSF RT-QuIC.

title: Two Months of Isolated Intractable Hiccups Followed by Acute Ophthalmoplegia, Bulbar Palsy, and Autonomic Instability Without Cutaneous Rash in a 35-Year-Old Man

presentation.chief_complaint: Intractable hiccups for 2 months followed by sudden progression to drowsiness, external ophthalmoplegia, facial diplegia, bulbar palsy, and severe autonomic storm without skin rash
presentation.history_of_present_illness: A 35-year-old immunocompetent man developed persistent, intractable hiccups and a dry cough following a period of psychological stress. Comprehensive gastroenterological and otolaryngological evaluations over 6 weeks were unremarkable. Seven weeks into his illness, he developed gait unsteadiness and dizziness, followed 3 days before admission by acute lethargy, dysarthria, facial asymmetry, dysphagia, and severe cardiovascular autonomic instability. He had no history of vesicular skin rash or dermatomal pain.
presentation.past_medical_history: Mild photosensitive dermatitis; no HIV, malignancy, or immunosuppressive therapy.
presentation.neuro_exam: Lethargic; bilateral ptosis, severe external ophthalmoplegia (limited left abduction and absent right adduction), peripheral left facial palsy, trismus, inability to protrude the tongue, absent gag and cough reflexes, and gait ataxia. Limb strength was 5/5 in all four extremities with normal deep tendon reflexes.
presentation.key_labs_csf: CSF analysis showed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis. CSF metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) DNA. Serum anti-ganglioside panel was positive for anti-GQ1b and anti-GM4 IgG antibodies. Serum AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG were negative.

imaging.modality: Multiparametric Axial Brain MRI at the Medulla Oblongata (T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI, ADC, T1+C)
imaging.caption: Axial brain MRI at the level of the medulla. The images demonstrate a lesion in the left medulla (white arrows) across different sequences: (A) T1-weighted image, (B) T2-weighted image, (C) FLAIR, (D) diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), (E) apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map and (F) contrast-enhanced T1-weighted image. The lesion shows hypointensity on T1, hyperintensity on T2 and FLAIR, isointensity on both DWI and the ADC map, and shows no contrast enhancement.
imaging.findings_summary: Well-demarcated non-enhancing T2/FLAIR hyperintense inflammatory lesion in the left dorsal medulla (involving the solitary tract, nucleus ambiguus, and hiccup reflex center) with normal DWI/ADC (excluding acute ischemic infarction).

challenge.question: What is the complete clinicopathological diagnosis for this patient presenting with prodromal intractable hiccups (dorsal medullary lesion, Figure 1) followed by drowsiness, external ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, positive serum anti-GQ1b antibodies, and VZV DNA in the CSF without rash?

options.text: Functional gastrointestinal hiccups — Reassure the patient and continue proton-pump inhibitor therapy
options.rationale: Incorrect. Intractable hiccups lasting >48 hours—especially when refractory to GI therapy—are a red flag for a structural or inflammatory lesion in the dorsal medulla (medullary hiccup center).

options.text: Acute Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Ischemic Infarction — Administer intravenous tenecteplase
options.rationale: Incorrect. The subacute 2-month progression of hiccups and the absence of diffusion restriction on DWI/ADC (Figure 1D–E) exclude an acute arterial ischemic stroke.

options.text: Ocular Myasthenia Gravis — Treat with oral pyridostigmine monotherapy
options.rationale: Incorrect. Myasthenia gravis does not cause a medullary T2/FLAIR lesion on MRI, CSF pleocytosis, central lethargy, or severe autonomic failure.

options.text: Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis (BBE) / Anti-GQ1b Antibody Syndrome triggered by Varicella-Zoster Virus reactivation without rash (Zoster Sine Herpete) — Requires combined IV Acyclovir + IVIG/Immunotherapy
options.rationale: Correct! Intractable hiccups localized to the dorsal medulla (nucleus tractus solitarius, nucleus ambiguus, and area postrema, Figure 1). Subsequent progression to drowsiness/stupor, external ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and positive serum anti-GQ1b IgG defines Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis (part of the anti-GQ1b spectrum alongside Miller Fisher syndrome). Detection of VZV DNA in CSF without cutaneous rash confirms Zoster Sine Herpete as the viral trigger, requiring concurrent high-dose IV acyclovir and immunomodulation (IVIG/corticosteroids).

resolution.final_diagnosis: Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis (BBE) and Anti-GQ1b Antibody Overlap Syndrome Triggered by Varicella-Zoster Virus Reactivation Without Rash (Zoster Sine Herpete)
resolution.clinical_discussion:
The central hiccup reflex arc integrates afferent signals from the vagus, phrenic, and sympathetic nerves within the dorsal medulla oblongata (specifically the nucleus tractus solitarius, nucleus ambiguus, reticular formation, and area postrema). Consequently, isolated intractable hiccups can be the sole heralding symptom of a life-threatening brainstem encephalitis or demyelinating disorder weeks before cranial neuropathies appear.

Anti-GQ1b IgG antibodies bind strongly to ganglioside epitopes enriched in the oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), and abducens (CN VI) nerves as well as the brainstem reticular formation, uniting Miller Fisher Syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia) and Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and impaired consciousness/pyramidal or bulbar signs) into a continuous clinicopathological spectrum. This landmark case demonstrates that Varicella-Zoster Virus reactivation without rash (zoster sine herpete) can directly invade the medulla and simultaneously trigger a fulminant secondary anti-GQ1b autoimmune response.
teaching_points: Intractable hiccups refractory to gastrointestinal therapy warrant Brain MRI with thin-slice medullary sequences to evaluate the dorsal medulla (nucleus tractus solitarius and area postrema).

The combination of external ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and impaired consciousness (drowsiness/coma) defines Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis (BBE), which is strongly associated with serum anti-GQ1b IgG antibodies.

Varicella-Zoster Virus can cause severe brainstem encephalitis in immunocompetent adults without any cutaneous rash (zoster sine herpete); concurrent CSF viral PCR/mNGS and autoimmune antibody testing are essential.
clinical_pitfalls: Assuming Varicella-Zoster Virus CNS infection is excluded simply because the patient is young, immunocompetent, and lacks a vesicular dermatomal rash.
Attributing persistent hiccups solely to gastroesophageal reflux or stress without performing a cranial nerve exam and posterior fossa MRI.
